title: The Buddha Speaks the Sutra on Contemplating the Buddha of Immeasurable Life: A Commentary
author: Commentary by Zhanran

blocks.text: Introduction
Preface

inline.s: The occasion of this sutra was that Queen Vaidehī, having suffered the calamity of an evil son who imprisoned his father and would have harmed his mother, grew grief-worn and haggard, and with all her heart pleaded with the Buddha to teach her the contemplation of the place of pure karma, and also so that all ordinary beings of future ages who wish to cultivate pure karma might be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. The World-Honored One therefore set forth the three blessings of pure karma as the direct cause of rebirth. Then by various skillful means he taught the sixteen wondrous contemplations, so that when her contemplation was accomplished she saw with her own eyes the splendor of the dependent and primary rewards of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, received the Buddha's prediction, purified and removed the karmic obstacles and the offenses of birth and death accumulated over countless kalpas, and was assured of rebirth at the end of life.
Contemplating the place of pure karma: the sutra says:
“I pray only that the Buddha-Sun teach me to contemplate the place of pure karma.”
Buddha-Sun: a reverent epithet for the Buddha, because the Buddha can dispel the darkness of delusion in living beings, just as the sun can dispel darkness.

In the practice of the Pure Land dharma-gate there are four ways of recollecting the Buddha: 1. Recollection by holding the name — single-mindedly invoking the Buddha's name; 2. Recollection by contemplating an image — gazing at a Buddha image while invoking the Buddha's name aloud; 3. Recollection by contemplation — visualizing in the mind the Buddha's marks and splendid adornments; 4. Recollection of the true aspect — contemplating the true aspect of one's own body and of all Buddhas, which is neither empty nor existent and yet both empty and existent, so that mind, Buddha, and living beings are three and yet without distinction.
This sutra begins with recollection by contemplation, sets out various contemplations, and finally leads to the most supremely excellent practice of holding the name. At the end of the sutra it says:
“The Buddha told Ānanda: Hold well these words! To hold these words is to hold the name of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life.”
(The Buddha tells Ānanda: you must earnestly uphold this sutra that I have taught! To uphold this sutra is to hold and recite the name of Amitābha Buddha.)
This sutra has two assemblies: one in the palace, where the World-Honored One taught in person; and one on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, where Ānanda proclaimed it again on the Buddha's behalf.

The whole sutra falls into three great parts: 1. the origin of the teaching and contemplation (the introductory part); 2. the sixteen contemplations (the main part); 3. upholding and transmitting it (the part on dissemination).

blocks.text: The Title of the Sutra

inline.s: The Buddha Speaks the Sutra on Contemplating the Buddha of Immeasurable Life

The title, “The Buddha Speaks the Sutra on Contemplating the Buddha of Immeasurable Life,” is made up of three parts: “The Buddha Speaks,” “Contemplating the Buddha of Immeasurable Life,” and “Sutra.” “Sutra” means a scripture, that is, an authoritative work. “The Buddha Speaks” marks this sutra as spoken by Śākyamuni Buddha. “Contemplating the Buddha of Immeasurable Life” tells how to contemplate the Buddha of Immeasurable Life and the dependent and primary adornments of the Land of Ultimate Bliss that he established. The Buddha of Immeasurable Life is Amitābha Buddha. “Amita” is a transliteration; “Immeasurable Life” translates the meaning.

Dependent and primary rewards: the dependent reward and the primary reward. Dependent reward: the karmic result of the environment on which one relies, such as lands and soil, houses and implements — that is, one's living environment. Primary reward: the body and mind of Buddhas and living beings; this is the true substance of the karmic result drawn forth by past karmic causes.

In this sutra, as to the dependent reward there are three kinds: 1. the adornments below the ground, namely the jeweled banners and lights beneath the lapis lazuli ground reflecting one another; 2. the adornments on the ground, namely all the jeweled lands, groves, ponds, towers, and pavilions; 3. the adornments in space, namely all the transforming jeweled palaces, pearl nets, flower clouds, manifested birds, pure breezes, and sounds of music. As to the primary reward there are two kinds: 1. the adornment of the lord, namely the Buddha of Immeasurable Life (Amitābha Buddha); 2. the adornment of the sages, namely the bodhisattvas, voice-hearers, gods, and humans of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

blocks.text: The Translator

inline.s: Translated by Tripiṭaka Master Kālayaśas of the Western Regions, Liu Song dynasty
Liu Song: in Chinese history there were two dynasties that took “Song” as their state name. One was one of the Southern Dynasties: in the year
Liu Yu proclaimed himself emperor, named the state Song, and made Jiankang (present-day Nanjing, Jiangsu) its capital. The other was in the year

, when Zhao Kuangyin (Emperor Taizu of Song) proclaimed himself emperor, named the state Song, and fixed its capital at Bianjing (present-day Kaifeng, Henan). The former is called “Liu Song,” the latter “Zhao Song.” Western Regions: from the Han dynasty onward, a general term for the region west of Yumen Pass in present-day Gansu. In the narrow sense it means the area east of the Pamirs; in the broad sense it refers generally to west and central Asia, the Indian subcontinent, and even Eastern Europe and North Africa. Tripiṭaka Master: “Tripiṭaka” means the three baskets — the basket of sutras, the basket of vinaya, and the basket of treatises. The basket of sutras is the scriptures spoken by the Buddha; the basket of vinaya is the precepts laid down by the Buddha; the basket of treatises is the treatises composed by the Buddha's disciples. A “Tripiṭaka Master” is a monk thoroughly versed in all three baskets of sutras, vinaya, and treatises. Kālayaśas (
jiāng
CE) was widely learned in the Abhidharma and the vinaya and skilled in meditative contemplation. In the first year of Yuanjia of Emperor Wen of Liu Song (

CE) he went from the Western Regions to Jiankang and stayed at the Daolin Retreat on Mount Zhong, where he translated the Sutra on Contemplating the Buddha of Immeasurable Life and the Sutra on Contemplating the Two Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajya-rāja and Bhaiṣajya-samudgata. In the nineteenth year of Yuanjia he traveled west to Min and Shu to spread the Dharma. He later passed away at Jiangling.

blocks.text: Main Content

inline.s: The main content of this sutra is the sixteen contemplations; hence it is also commonly called the Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations.
The sixteen contemplations: sixteen kinds of visualization:
) Contemplation of the Sun: single-mindedly and closely contemplate the setting sun in the west, hanging like a suspended drum. (
) Contemplation of Water: calm the mind and visualize the waters of the west freezing into ice, pure and radiant, like lapis lazuli. (
) Contemplation of the Ground: with one mind closely contemplate the lapis lazuli jeweled ground of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, clear within and without, pure and adorned. (
) Contemplation of Trees: with one mind visualize the seven rows of trees, made of many jewels, their branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit interwoven of the eight precious substances. (
) Contemplation of the Water of Eight Qualities: single-mindedly and closely contemplate the water of eight qualities, like a wish-fulfilling pearl, flowing among the flowers. (

) Comprehensive Contemplation: with one mind visualize the Land of Ultimate Bliss, made of many jewels, its pavilions, terraces, and towers, the assembled heavenly beings performing heavenly music and ever recollecting the Three Jewels. (

) Contemplation of the Flower Throne: with one mind closely contemplate, above the pool of seven jewels, the hundred-jewel flower terrace and the wondrous pearl net adorning the vajra jewel throne, which transforms as the mind wills and accomplishes the great Buddha-work.

) Contemplation of the Jeweled Image: with one mind visualize Amitābha Buddha seated on a lotus terrace, with the two great bodhisattvas Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta standing in attendance to left and right, emitting great radiance that illumines the ten directions. Water, birds, and trees all proclaim the wondrous Dharma. (

) Contemplation of the Buddha's Body: with one mind closely contemplate the bodily marks and radiance of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life — the white tuft of hair curling like five Mount Sumerus, the deep blue eyes clear as the four great oceans. Within his bodily marks one sees throughout the ten directions countless Buddhas. (

) Contemplation of Avalokiteśvara: with one mind closely contemplate Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara — his ushnisha and halo, his purple-gold body, his majestic marks and adornments, freely transforming and filling the whole dharma-realm. (

) Contemplation of Mahāsthāmaprāpta: with one mind closely contemplate Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta — his purple-gold body and all-illumining halo; within the light of a single pore one sees throughout the ten directions countless Buddhas. When this bodhisattva walks, the earth trembles throughout the worlds of the ten directions. (

) Universal Visualization: with one mind visualize oneself already born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, sitting cross-legged within a lotus. When the lotus opens, five hundred kinds of light shine upon and touch my body, and I see Buddhas and bodhisattvas filling the sky. The sounds issued by water, birds, and groves, and by the Buddhas, all proclaim the wondrous Dharma. (

) Miscellaneous Visualization: with one mind visualize Amitābha Buddha, freely exercising his spiritual powers, manifesting in the lands of the ten directions according to the kind of being. The three holy ones appear together, great and small without obstruction, seated on jeweled lotuses.

) Contemplation of Birth in the Upper Grades: with one mind contemplate the causes of rebirth, the circumstances of rebirth, and the benefits after rebirth of the three kinds of people — those of upper grade upper birth, upper grade middle birth, and upper grade lower birth. (

) Contemplation of Birth in the Middle Grades: with one mind contemplate the causes of rebirth, the circumstances of rebirth, and the benefits after rebirth of the three kinds of people — those of middle grade upper birth, middle grade middle birth, and middle grade lower birth. (

) Contemplation of Birth in the Lower Grades: with one mind contemplate the causes of rebirth, the circumstances of rebirth, and the benefits after rebirth of the three kinds of people — those of lower grade upper birth, lower grade middle birth, and lower grade lower birth.

blocks.text: 1. The Origin of the Teaching and Contemplation

inline.s: This chapter is the introductory part of the sutra; it relates how the World-Honored One came to teach Ānanda and Vaidehī the sixteen contemplations.

blocks.text: 1. The Holy Assembly

inline.s: Thus have I heard:
I (Ānanda) heard the Buddha say this with my own ears:

Thus have I heard: I (Ānanda) heard the Buddha say this with my own ears. This sutra was repeated by Ānanda, a disciple of Śākyamuni Buddha, when the scriptures were compiled. Ānanda: in full, Ānanda, one of the Buddha's ten great disciples. He was the Buddha's cousin, born on the night of the Buddha's enlightenment; he later left home to follow the Buddha, attended him for twenty-five years, and served as his personal attendant. He was renowned as foremost in hearing much, and many scriptures were repeated by him at the compilations. The ten great disciples: the ten chief disciples of Śākyamuni Buddha, namely: Śāriputra, foremost in wisdom; Maudgalyāyana, foremost in spiritual powers; Subhūti, foremost in understanding emptiness; Ānanda, foremost in hearing much; Upāli, foremost in upholding the precepts; Aniruddha, foremost in the divine eye; Mahākāśyapa, foremost in ascetic practices; Pūrṇa, foremost in expounding the Dharma; Kātyāyana, foremost in discussion; and Rāhula, foremost in secret practice. Ascetic practices: a course of practice that casts off the three attachments to clothing, food, and dwelling. One who cultivates ascetic practices must observe twelve rules, called the “twelve dhūta practices.”

At one time the Buddha was on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of monks, twelve hundred and fifty in all. There were also thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas, with the Dharma-prince Mañjuśrī as their leader.

At that time Śākyamuni Buddha was on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of monks, twelve hundred and fifty in number. There were thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas, with Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī as their leader.

At one time: at that time. Rājagṛha: the capital of the kingdom of Magadha in central India. Gṛdhrakūṭa: also translated as Vulture Peak or Spirit Mountain, situated to the northeast of Rājagṛha; it was a famous resort where the Buddha often taught the Dharma. Monk (bhikṣu): a man who has left home and received full ordination. Full ordination precepts: the complete and perfect precepts — two hundred and fifty for monks and three hundred and forty-eight for nuns. Great monks: a description indicating that these monks were of high attainment in practice. Together: in one place. Foremost: the one of highest rank in the assembly. The Dharma-prince Mañjuśrī: Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī. Dharma-prince: an honorific for great bodhisattvas, because great bodhisattvas are born into the family of the Dharma-king (the Buddha) and are able to carry on the Buddha-Dharma.

blocks.text: 2. Imprisoning the Father and Harming the Mother

inline.s: At that time in the great city of Rājagṛha there was a prince named Ajātaśatru, who, following the instructions of his evil friend Devadatta, arrested his father King Bimbisāra and shut him up in a chamber with seven walls, ordering all his ministers that not one of them was to go there.

At that time in the great city of Rājagṛha there was a prince named Ajātaśatru, who, trusting and following the instigations of his evil friend Devadatta (Diaoda), usurped the throne. He shut his father King Bimbisāra in a chamber with seven walls, intending to starve him to death, and strictly forbade all the ministers to visit him.
Diaoda: in full, Devadatta. He was a son of King Droṇodana (
hú

), a cousin of Śākyamuni Buddha and the elder brother of Ānanda. He had thirty of the marks. Because he saw that kings and ministers all took refuge in and looked up to the World-Honored One, and that offerings overflowed, he grew envious; he went to the Buddha and asked to be allowed to lead the assembly. Rebuked by the Buddha, he plotted to harm him. He asked Ānanda to transmit to him the methods of spiritual power, and Ānanda, not understanding the situation, transmitted them. He entered the mountains to practice and gained the five spiritual powers. Then he secretly reasoned: who shall be my great patron? Prince Ajātaśatru has the marks of a great king and is the most suitable. So he displayed various miraculous transformations to bewitch the prince into believing in him, and said to the prince: ‘I shall be the new Buddha and you the new king — how excellent that would be!’ Thereupon the prince usurped the throne, imprisoned his father, and meant to starve him to death. The five spiritual powers: also called the five superknowledges, namely: the divine eye, the divine ear, the knowledge of others' minds, the recollection of past lives, and the power of unimpeded transformation.

The queen mother, named Vaidehī, was reverent toward the king. Having bathed and purified herself, she smeared her body with ghee, honey, and parched flour, filled her necklaces with grape juice, and secretly brought them to the king.

The prince's mother, the queen mother, was named Vaidehī, and she remained deeply reverent toward King Bimbisāra. After bathing and purifying herself, she mixed ghee and honey with parched flour and smeared it over her body, and she put grape juice in her necklaces and secretly brought it to the king to eat.
Parched flour (
chǎo
): roasted flour. Necklace of jewels: an ornament strung of pearls and jade in ancient times, most often worn at the neck.

Then the king ate the parched flour and drank the juice, and asked for water to rinse his mouth. When he had rinsed his mouth, he joined his palms in reverence, faced Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, bowed from afar to the World-Honored One, and said: ‘Mahāmaudgalyāyana, you are my dear friend; be so compassionate as to give me the eight precepts.’

At that time the king finished the parched flour mixed with ghee and honey and drank the grape juice, then asked for water to rinse his mouth. When he had rinsed his mouth, he joined his palms and, facing Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in reverence, bowed from afar to the World-Honored One and said: ‘Mahāmaudgalyāyana, you are my intimate friend; I pray you raise a compassionate mind and give me the eight precepts of the fast day.’

The eight precepts: also called the eight precepts of the fast day. 1. Not to kill: not to kill living creatures. 2. Not to take what is not given: not to take what others have not given. 3. Not to practice unchastity: not to engage in sexual union. 4. Not to speak falsely: not to speak words contrary to fact. 5. Not to drink alcohol: not to drink any kind of liquor. 6. Not to adorn oneself with garlands, nor to dance, sing, or watch and listen: not to anoint the body with perfumes or wear flower garlands, and not to watch dancing or listen to singing. 7. Not to sleep or sit on high, broad, luxurious beds: not to sit or lie on a high, broad, and splendid bed. 8. Not to eat at improper times: not to eat food at improper times, that is, not to eat after noon. Abstaining from these eight wrong practices constitutes the eight precepts; and because the eighth of them, abstaining from food at improper times, is a rule of fasting, the whole set is called the eight precepts of the fast. Not eating after noon: from the time the sun passes high noon until the following dawn, no food may be eaten.

Then Maudgalyāyana, flying like a hawk or falcon, swiftly came to where the king was, and day after day he did the same, giving the king the eight precepts. The World-Honored One also sent the venerable Pūrṇa to teach the Dharma to the king. Thus twenty-one days passed; because the king ate the parched flour and honey and heard the Dharma, his countenance was peaceful and joyful.

At that time Maudgalyāyana, flying like an eagle or vulture, swiftly came to the king's dwelling; day after day he did the same, giving the king the eight precepts of the fast day. The World-Honored One also sent the venerable Pūrṇa to teach the Dharma to the king. Twenty-one days (three times seven) thus passed, and because the king ate parched flour with ghee and honey, drank grape juice, upheld the fasting precepts, and heard the Dharma, his countenance became healthy and peaceful.
Hawk and falcon (
sǔn

): hawks and vultures. Maudgalyāyana: Mahāmaudgalyāyana, also called Great Maudgalyāyana, or simply Maudgalyāyana or Mulian, one of the Buddha's ten great disciples, renowned as foremost in spiritual powers. Pūrṇa: one of the Buddha's ten great disciples, renowned as foremost in expounding the Dharma. Day after day he did the same, giving the king the eight precepts: the eight precepts are a set of precepts to be upheld for one day and one night. As the text of the precepts says: ‘The first, not to kill, is the precept of the eightfold fast-day observance — can you uphold it for one day and one night?’ In this way each item is asked: ‘Can you uphold it for one day and one night?’ The answer is: ‘I can uphold it,’ which means that one has accepted this set of precepts. The precept-body of the eight precepts lasts only one day and one night; when dawn comes the next day, the precept-body naturally ceases. Hence, ‘day after day he did the same, giving the king the eight precepts.’

Then Ajātaśatru asked the gatekeeper: ‘Is my father the king still alive now?’ The gatekeeper replied: ‘Great king, the queen mother smears her body with parched flour and honey and fills her necklaces with juice, and brings them to the former king. The ascetics Maudgalyāyana and Pūrṇa come through the air and teach the Dharma to the former king; they cannot be restrained.’

At that time Ajātaśatru asked the gatekeeper: ‘Is my father the king still alive?’ Thereupon the gatekeeper reported: ‘Great king, the queen mother smears her body with parched flour mixed with ghee and honey, and fills her necklaces with grape juice, and brings them for the former king to eat. The ascetics Maudgalyāyana and Pūrṇa come through the air and teach the Dharma to the former king; there is no way to restrain them.’
To address reverently: to speak respectfully, as a junior to a senior or a subordinate to a superior.

When Ajātaśatru heard these words, he was enraged at his mother and said: ‘My mother is a thief, a companion of thieves. Those wicked ascetics, with their spells and sorcery, keep this wicked king alive for many days.’ Thereupon he seized a sharp sword and meant to harm his mother.

When Ajātaśatru heard this, he was furious with his mother and said: ‘My mother is a thief, a companion of thieves. Those wicked ascetics, with their spells and sorcery, keep this wicked king alive for many days.’ At once he grasped a sharp sword and wanted to kill his mother.

Then there was a minister named Candraprabha (Moonlight), wise and intelligent, who together with Jīvaka bowed to the king and said: ‘Great king, we have heard the Veda scriptures say that since the beginning of the kalpa there have been wicked kings who, greedy for the throne, killed their fathers — eighteen thousand of them. But never have we heard of one who, devoid of principle, harmed his mother. That the king should now commit this parricidal act defiles the kṣatriya race; we cannot bear to hear of it. This is the conduct of an outcaste; it is not fitting for us to remain here any longer.’ When the two ministers had said this, they laid their hands on their swords and withdrew backwards.

At that time there was a minister named Moonlight, wise and intelligent, who together with another minister, Jīvaka, bowed to Ajātaśatru and said: ‘Great king, we have heard the Veda scriptures say: “Since the beginning of the kalpa there have been wicked kings who, greedy for the throne, killed their fathers — eighteen thousand of them.” Yet never have we heard of anyone cruelly and unjustly killing his mother. That the king should now commit this parricidal act defiles the kṣatriya race; we cannot bear to see or hear it. This is the conduct of a śūdra (outcaste); it is not fitting for us to remain here any longer.’ When the two ministers had spoken these words, they laid their hands on their swords and stepped backwards, ready to leave.

Kṣatriya: that is, the kṣatriya caste. The four castes: brahmin, kṣatriya, vaiśya, and śūdra. The brahmins were the priests of ancient India and held the highest authority; the kṣatriyas were the royal caste, honored as highly as the brahmins; the vaiśyas were the ordinary class of farmers, workers, and merchants; the śūdras were slaves made to serve others.
Then Ajātaśatru, alarmed and frightened, said to Jīvaka: ‘Will you not stand by me?’ Jīvaka replied: ‘Great king, take care not to harm your mother!’

At that time Ajātaśatru, seeing that the two trusted ministers who held great power were about to leave him, was alarmed and frightened, and said to Jīvaka and the other: ‘Will you no longer follow me?’ Jīvaka said: ‘Great king, by no means harm your mother!’

When the king heard these words, he repented and begged their pardon; he at once threw down the sword and ceased to harm his mother. He ordered the palace attendants: ‘Shut her in the inner palace and let her not come out again.’

When Ajātaśatru heard this, he at once repented and asked their forgiveness, threw down the sword, and did not kill his mother. But he ordered the palace attendants: ‘Confine the queen mother in the inner palace and do not let her go out!’

blocks.text: 3. Praying for the Buddha's Instruction

inline.s: At that time, after Vaidehī had been shut up, she was grief-stricken and haggard. Facing Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa from afar, she bowed to the Buddha and said: ‘Tathāgata, World-Honored One, in former days you always sent Ānanda to comfort me. Now I am grieving, and the World-Honored One in his august majesty is beyond my reach. I pray you send Maudgalyāyana and the venerable Ānanda to see me.’ Having said this, she wept bitterly, her tears falling like rain, and bowed from afar to the Buddha.

At that time, after Vaidehī was shut up, she was grief-stricken and haggard. Facing Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa from afar, she bowed to the Buddha and said: ‘Tathāgata, World-Honored One, in times past you always sent Ānanda to comfort me. Now I am grieving, and the World-Honored One in his august majesty is beyond my reach. I pray you send the venerable Maudgalyāyana and Ānanda to see me.’ When she had said this, she wept without cease, her tears falling like rain, and bowed from afar to the World-Honored One.

Before she could raise her head, the World-Honored One on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa knew what Vaidehī was thinking and at once commanded Mahāmaudgalyāyana and Ānanda to come through the air. The Buddha himself vanished from Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and appeared in the royal palace.

Before Vaidehī had raised her head, the World-Honored One on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa knew what was in her mind and at once commanded Maudgalyāyana and Ānanda to come through the air. The Buddha himself vanished from Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and appeared in the royal palace.

When Vaidehī had bowed and raised her head, she saw the World-Honored One, Śākyamuni Buddha, his body purple-gold in color, seated on a hundred-jewel lotus. Maudgalyāyana attended on his left and Ānanda on his right, while Śakra, Brahmā, and the world-protecting gods in the sky rained down heavenly flowers and offered them in homage.

When Vaidehī raised her head, she saw the World-Honored One, Śākyamuni Buddha, his body purple-gold in color, seated on a hundred-jewel lotus throne. Maudgalyāyana attended on his left and Ānanda on his right, while the king of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, the great Brahmā king, and the four world-protecting kings in the sky rained down heavenly flowers and offered them to the Buddha.

Śakra: the lord of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven. Brahmā king: in the first dhyāna heaven of the form realm there are three heavens — the heaven of Brahmā's retinue, the heaven of Brahmā's ministers, and the heaven of Great Brahmā — and the lord of the heaven of Great Brahmā is called the Brahmā king. The four world-protecting kings: the four heavenly kings are Dhṛtarāṣṭra (Holder of the Realm), Virūḍhaka (Increase and Growth), Virūpākṣa (Broad Eyes), and Vaiśravaṇa (Much Hearing). Because these four heavenly kings are good deities who guard the world, they are called the “four world-protecting kings.”

Then Vaidehī, seeing the Buddha, the World-Honored One, tore off her necklaces, threw herself to the ground, and weeping aloud before the Buddha said: ‘World-Honored One, what offense did I commit in past lives that I should bear this evil son? World-Honored One, what karmic cause is there that you should be kin with Devadatta?

At that time Vaidehī, seeing the World-Honored One, in her agitation tore off her necklaces, threw herself to the ground, and weeping aloud before the Buddha said reverently: ‘World-Honored One, what karma did I commit in the past that I should have borne such an evil son? World-Honored One, what cause is there that you should be kin with Devadatta?

Tearing off her necklaces: the necklaces were jewels adorning her body; she tore them off with her own hands and cast aside these ornaments, so extreme was her grief and indignation and so great her pain.

I pray only that the World-Honored One broadly teach me of a place free of sorrow and affliction, where I may be reborn; I take no joy in this defiled and evil world of Jambudvīpa! This defiled and evil place is filled with hells, hungry ghosts, and animals, and is crowded with the unwholesome. May I in the future hear no evil sound and see no evil person. Now I bow to the World-Honored One with all five limbs to the ground and beg for compassion and repentance. I pray only that the Buddha-Sun teach me to contemplate the place of pure karma.’

I pray only that the World-Honored One broadly teach me of a place free of sorrow and affliction, and I will be reborn there; I do not wish to remain in this defiled and evil world of Jambudvīpa! This defiled and evil place is filled with hells, hungry ghosts, and animals, and is mostly a gathering of the unwholesome. May I in the future hear no evil sound and see no evil person. Now I bow with all five limbs to the ground before the World-Honored One, seeking compassion and repentance. I pray only that the World-Honored One teach me to contemplate the place of pure karma.’

Jambudvīpa: translated into Chinese as “the continent of the rose-apple tree.” It is the Sahā world in which we now dwell. Bowing with all five limbs to the ground: this is the highest form of reverence — both hands, both knees, and the crown of the head touching the ground. Buddha-Sun: a reverent epithet for the Buddha, because the Buddha can dispel the darkness of delusion in living beings, just as the sun can dispel darkness. Teach me to contemplate the place of pure karma: Vaidehī asked the Buddha to teach her the contemplation of “the place of pure karma.” Therefore, in answer to her request, the World-Honored One taught the first thirteen contemplations of “the place of pure karma” (from the contemplation of the sun through the miscellaneous visualization). Then, without being asked, he went on to teach the last three contemplations of the marks of rebirth (birth in the upper, middle, and lower grades), and in a culminating stroke revealed the incomparably supreme dharma-gate of holding the Buddha's name.

blocks.text: 4. The Vow to Be Born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss

inline.s: Then the World-Honored One emitted light from between his brows. The light was golden and illumined the countless worlds of the ten directions. It returned and rested on the Buddha's crown, where it transformed into a golden platform like Mount Sumeru, and within it appeared all the pure and wondrous lands of the Buddhas of the ten directions: some lands were made of the seven treasures; some lands were wholly of lotuses; some lands were like the palace of the Heaven of Free Enjoyment; some lands were like a crystal mirror, in which the lands of the ten directions all appeared. There were countless Buddha-lands such as these, splendid and wonderful to behold, and the Buddha let Vaidehī see them.

At that time the World-Honored One emitted light from between his brows. The light was golden and illumined the countless worlds of the ten directions. The golden light returned and rested on the Buddha's crown, where it transformed into a golden platform as great as Mount Sumeru, and within it appeared all the pure and wondrous lands of the Buddhas of the ten directions: some lands were made of the seven treasures; some lands were wholly of lotuses; some lands were like the palace of the Heaven of Free Enjoyment; some lands were like a glass mirror, in which the lands of the ten directions all appeared. There were countless Buddha-lands such as these, all of them utterly splendid and glorious, and the World-Honored One let Vaidehī behold them one by one.

Palace of the Heaven of Free Enjoyment: the fourth heaven of the four dhyāna heavens of the form realm, the palace of the lord of the Heaven of Free Enjoyment. The character li: in this context the same as “glass” (boli).

Then Vaidehī said to the Buddha: ‘World-Honored One, these Buddha-lands, though pure, all have light. But I now wish to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, where Amitābha Buddha dwells. I pray only that the World-Honored One teach me reflective thinking and teach me right absorption.’

At that time Vaidehī said to the Buddha: ‘World-Honored One, all these Buddha-lands, though pure, all have light. But I now wish to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, the realm of Amitābha Buddha. I pray only that the World-Honored One teach me reflective thinking and teach me right absorption.’

Reflective thinking: recollection with a still-scattered mind is called reflective thinking. Right absorption: the meditative concentration in which thought is stilled and the mind is gathered is called “right absorption.”

Then the World-Honored One smiled, and five-colored light issued from the Buddha's mouth, each ray of light falling on the crown of King Bimbisāra's head. At that time the king, though imprisoned, had no obstruction in his mind's eye, and seeing the World-Honored One from afar, he bowed his head and face to the ground; his merit naturally increased, and he attained the fruit of Anāgāmin.

At that time the World-Honored One at once smiled with delight, and five-colored light issued from the Buddha's mouth, each ray of light falling on the crown of King Bimbisāra's head. At that time, through the blessing of the Buddha's light, King Bimbisāra, though his body was imprisoned, had no obstruction in his mind's eye and saw the World-Honored One from afar. He at once bowed his head and face to the ground, and his merit naturally increased,
attaining the fruit of Anāgāmin

Mind's eye: by the power of meditative concentration one can see through forms beyond obstacles and clearly perceive all dharmas. This relies neither on the physical eye nor on the divine eye; by the power of concentration one can illuminate the Buddhas and the splendor of Buddha-lands in other directions, or become aware of the various impurities within one's own body. Bowing with head and face: touching the ground with one's own head and face in reverence for the feet of a venerable one. Anāgāmin: translated as “non-returner,” meaning that one who attains this fruit will in the future be born in the form realm or the formless realm and will no longer return to the desire realm to undergo birth and death. This is the third fruit of the voice-hearer vehicle; see the note on the “four fruits of the voice-hearer” below.

blocks.text: 5. The Three Blessings to Be Cultivated

inline.s: Then the World-Honored One said to Vaidehī: Do you know? Amitābha Buddha is not far from here. You should bind your thoughts and closely contemplate those in that land who have accomplished pure karma. I will now for your sake set forth many parables, and also cause all ordinary beings of future ages who wish to cultivate pure karma to be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

At that time the World-Honored One said to Vaidehī: Do you know? Amitābha Buddha is not far from here. You should bind your thoughts and closely contemplate (visualize carefully) the dependent and primary adornments of that land (the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss), accomplished through pure karma. I will now for your sake set forth many parables, and also cause all ordinary beings of future ages who wish to cultivate pure karma to be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Those who wish to be born in that land should cultivate three blessings: first, to be filial and support one's parents, to serve and respect teachers and elders, to be compassionate and refrain from killing, and to cultivate the ten wholesome actions; second, to receive and uphold the three refuges, to fulfill all the precepts, and not to transgress the rules of demeanor; third, to arouse the bodhi-mind, to deeply believe in cause and effect, to read and recite the Mahāyāna scriptures, and to encourage others to practice. These three matters are called pure karma.

Those who wish to be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss must cultivate three blessings: 1. to be filial and support one's parents, to serve and respect teachers and elders, to be compassionate and refrain from killing, and to cultivate the ten wholesome actions; 2. to receive and uphold the three refuges, to fulfill all the precepts, and not to transgress the rules of demeanor; 3. to arouse the bodhi-mind, to deeply believe in cause and effect, to read and recite the Mahāyāna scriptures, and to encourage and urge on practitioners. These three matters are called pure karma.

The ten wholesome actions: the ten kinds of wholesome karma — not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct, not speaking falsely, not speaking divisively (not sowing discord), not speaking harshly (not mocking with evil words), not speaking idly (not speaking meaningless words), not being greedy, not being hateful, and not being deluded (not going against the truth). (For details see
Notes on the Sutra of the Ten Wholesome Ways of Action

) The three refuges: that is, taking refuge in the Buddha, taking refuge in the Dharma, and taking refuge in the Sangha. This is taking refuge in the Three Jewels: the Buddhas are the Jewel of the Buddha, the true Dharma is the Jewel of the Dharma, and the community of noble and holy ones (voice-hearers, solitary realizers, and bodhisattvas who receive the Buddha's teaching, cultivate the causes, and attain the fruits) is the Jewel of the Sangha. Rules of demeanor: the dignified bearing and rules proper to walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. Arousing the bodhi-mind: arousing the great mind that seeks the Buddha-path above (to become a Buddha) and transforms living beings below.

[The Three Vehicles] The Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Bodhisattva vehicle. The Śrāvaka vehicle, also called the Lesser Vehicle, whose practitioner, in as few as three lives or as many as sixty kalpas, cultivates the contemplation of emptiness and at last, hearing the Tathāgata’s voice teaching, awakens to the truth of the Four Noble Truths, cuts off the delusions of false views and false thinking, and attains the fruit of arhatship. The Pratyekabuddha vehicle, also called the Middle Vehicle, whose practitioner, in as few as four lives or as many as a hundred kalpas, breaks through ignorance and at last awakens to the truth of the twelve links of dependent origination, and attains the fruit of the pratyekabuddha. The Bodhisattva vehicle, also called the Great Vehicle, whose practitioner, over countless kalpas, practices the six perfections and, over further hundreds of kalpas, plants the karmic causes of the thirty-two marks, and attains the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood. [The Six Perfections] The six practices by which one may cross from this shore of the suffering of birth and death to the other shore of the bliss of nirvāṇa. Namely: giving, morality, patience, vigor, meditation, and prajñā. Giving can overcome greed and miserliness; morality can overcome transgression; patience can overcome hatred and anger; vigor can overcome indolence; meditation can overcome distraction; prajñā can overcome ignorance.
[The Buddha told Vaidehī: Do you know now? These three kinds of action are the primary cause of pure karma of the Buddhas of the past, the future, and the present of the three times.]
The Buddha told Vaidehī: Do you know that these three kinds of action are the primary cause of the pure karma of the Buddhas of the past, the future, and the present of the three times?
[Pure karma] Pure and wholesome karmic action. [Primary cause] The principal cause is called the “primary cause”; a secondary contributory condition is called the “conditional cause.”

blocks.text: Six. How Shall They See It

inline.s: [The Buddha told Ānanda and Vaidehī: Listen! Listen! Think on it well! The Tathāgata now, for the sake of all sentient beings of future ages who are harmed by the thief of afflictions, speaks the pure karma.]

The Buddha said to Ānanda and Vaidehī: Listen (listen attentively)! Listen! Think on it well! I now, for the sake of all sentient beings of future ages who are harmed by the thief of afflictions, speak the pure karma.

[Well done! Vaidehī, you have asked well about this matter. Ānanda, you should accept and uphold this and widely proclaim the Buddha’s words to the many. The Tathāgata now teaches Vaidehī and all sentient beings of future ages to contemplate the Western Land of Utmost Bliss. By the Buddha’s power, they shall see that pure land, just as one holds a bright mirror and sees one’s own face. Seeing the supremely wonderful and blissful things of that land, and being joyful in heart, at once one attains the patient endurance of the non-arising of phenomena.]

Very good! Vaidehī, I am pleased that you ask how to think and how to rightly receive, so as to be reborn in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss. Ānanda, you should accept and uphold the teaching I now give and widely proclaim the Buddha’s words to the many. I now teach Vaidehī and all sentient beings of future ages to contemplate the Western Land of Utmost Bliss. Because of the power of the Buddha’s aid, they shall see that pure land, just as one holds a bright mirror and sees one’s own face. Seeing the supremely wonderful and blissful things of that land, and being joyful in heart, one at once attains the patient endurance of the non-arising of phenomena.’

[You have asked well about this matter] I am pleased that you ask how to think and how to rightly receive, so as to be reborn in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss. It was said above that Vaidehī addressed the Buddha:
“I now delight to be born in the Land of Utmost Bliss in the presence of Amitābha Buddha. I only wish the World-honored One would teach me to think, and teach me to rightly receive.

[Patient endurance of the non-arising of phenomena] To penetrate that all phenomena are originally unproduced, whether sentient or non-sentient, all being dependently arisen and devoid of inherent nature, and thus in the midst of dharma without inherent nature, one’s mind of patient endurance is unmoved, and one personally realizes the non-arising.
[The Buddha told Vaidehī: You are an ordinary being; your thought and contemplation are weak
léi
and feeble — you have not obtained the divine eye and cannot contemplate from afar. The Buddhas and Tathāgatas have a special means by which you shall see.]

The Buddha told Vaidehī: You are an ordinary being; the power of your contemplative thought is lowly and weak, and you have not obtained the divine eye of transcendental vision, so you cannot from afar contemplate the Western Land of Utmost Bliss. The Buddhas and Tathāgatas have a special means by which you shall see.’

[The divine eye of transcendental vision] Whether far or near, within or without, day or night, all can be seen. [The Buddhas and Tathāgatas have a special means by which you shall see] This is what was said above: in the golden light at the Buddha’s crown appear the pure and wondrous lands of the Buddhas of the ten directions.

[At that time Vaidehī addressed the Buddha: World-honored One, as I now, by the Buddha’s power, see that land. If after the Buddha’s passing, all sentient beings, defiled, evil, and unwholesome, oppressed by the five sufferings, how shall they see the Land of Utmost Bliss of Amitābha Buddha?]

At that time Vaidehī addressed the Buddha: World-honored One, I now, by the Buddha’s power, in the golden light at the Buddha’s crown, see that land (the Western Land of Utmost Bliss). If after the Buddha’s passing, all sentient beings, defiled, evil, and unwholesome, oppressed by the five sufferings, how can they see the Land of Utmost Bliss of Amitābha Buddha?

[The five sufferings] First, the suffering of birth, aging, sickness, and death (the four inevitable processes of human life). Second, the suffering of separation from the beloved. Third, the suffering of meeting the hated. Fourth, the suffering of not obtaining what is sought. Fifth, the suffering of the raging of the five aggregates. [The five aggregates] Namely the five skandhas. [The five skandhas] The form aggregate, the feeling aggregate, the perception aggregate, the formation aggregate, and the consciousness aggregate. These five, being accumulated and arisen, are called the “five skandhas”; also, because they can cover a person’s true nature, causing delusion and inversion and the doing of all karmic deeds, they are also called the “five aggregates.” Among them, the form aggregate refers to matter and is called the “dharma of form”; the four aggregates of feeling, perception, formation, and consciousness belong to the mind and are called the “dharma of mind.” These are the five great elements that make up body and mind. Among them, the form aggregate is the physical body, and the remaining four aggregates (feeling, perception, formation, consciousness) are the mind.

blocks.text: Two. The Sixteen Contemplations

inline.s: This chapter is the main body of this sutra, and sets forth the sixteen contemplations.
In the text above, Vaidehī asked the Buddha:
“If after the Buddha’s passing, all sentient beings, defiled, evil, and unwholesome, oppressed by the five sufferings, how shall they see the Land of Utmost Bliss of Amitābha Buddha?”
Therefore the World-honored One instructed: sentient beings after the Buddha’s passing can, through the following various contemplations, see the Western Land of Utmost Bliss.
Master Hanshan says:
“Though
(although)
single-minded and exclusive recitation is indeed the proper practice, one must also rely upon contemplation, and it is then seen as even more secure and precise
(even more reliable and thorough)

. The Buddha, for Vaidehī, spoke the sixteen wondrous contemplations, so that in one lifetime success could be accomplished. Now the Contemplation Sutra is extant; if one forms pure companionships and cultivates together, letting each follow his own wish, then among the sixteen contemplations, take any one. Either contemplate the Buddha alone and the auspicious marks of the bodhisattvas, or contemplate the Pure Land state, such as the lotus and jewel ground spoken of in the Amitābha Sutra, contemplating as one wishes. If the contemplation is clear and distinct, then throughout the six periods of the day and night,
present before one as if in the Pure Land
, whether sitting, lying, walking, or standing, with eyes open or closed, it is as if before one’s eyes. If this contemplation is accomplished, at the moment of death, in one thought one is reborn.”
(Dream Wanderings Collection

Showing the Method of Cultivating the Pure Land Dharma Gate) [Among the sixteen contemplations, take any one] For example, single-mindedly contemplate oneself as already reborn in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss, sitting cross-legged within a lotus flower. When the lotus opens, five hundred rays of light touch my body, and I see Buddhas and bodhisattvas filling the sky. The water, birds, trees, and the sounds that issue from the Buddhas all proclaim the wondrous Dharma. (See later the “Universal Contemplation.”)

blocks.text: One. The Contemplation of the Sun

inline.s: [The Buddha told Vaidehī: You and all sentient beings should single-mindedly concentrate on one object and contemplate the West. How is the contemplation made? Whoever makes the contemplation, unless born blind, all with eyes have seen the sun set.]

The Buddha told Vaidehī: You and all sentient beings should single-mindedly concentrate on one object and contemplate the West. How is the contemplation made? Whoever makes the contemplation, provided one is not born blind (blind from birth), has seen the sun set.

[One should then give rise to this thought: sit upright facing west, contemplate intently the place where the sun is about to set, so that the mind abides firmly there, concentrated and unwavering. Beholding the sun about to set, its form like a suspended drum. Having seen the sun, whether the eyes are closed or open, make it clear and distinct. This is called the contemplation of the sun, the first contemplation.]

One should thus give rise to a thought: sit upright facing west, and contemplate intently (carefully observe) the place where the sun is about to set, causing the mind to abide firmly there, concentrated and unwavering. In the contemplation, see the setting sun about to sink, like a drum suspended at the edge of the sky. Having seen the setting sun in the contemplation, whether the eyes are closed or open, contemplate it all clearly and distinctly. This is called the contemplation of the sun, named the first contemplation.

blocks.text: Two. The Contemplation of Water

inline.s: [Next, make the contemplation of water. Beholding the water clear and pure, make it also clear and distinct, without a distracted mind. Having seen the water, one should then give rise to the contemplation of ice. Beholding the ice translucent, make the contemplation of crystal.]

Next, make the contemplation of water. In the contemplation, see the water clear and pure, and see it thoroughly clear and distinct, without a distracted mind. After having seen the water, one should give rise to the contemplation of ice, seeing the water freeze into ice. Take the translucent and clear ice as the object of the contemplation of crystal.

blocks.text: Three. The Contemplation of the Ground

inline.s: [When this contemplation is accomplished, one sees the crystal ground, translucent within and without, below which is a pillar of vajra and the seven treasures supporting the crystal ground. That pillar has eight sides, with eight ridges complete. Each side is made of a hundred treasures. Each jewel has a thousand rays of light; each ray of light, having eighty-four thousand colors reflecting on the crystal ground, like a billion suns, cannot be seen in full.]

When this contemplation is accomplished, one sees the emerald crystal ground, translucent within and without, below which is a golden pillar inlaid with vajra and the seven treasures, supporting the crystal ground. The vajra jewel-pillar has eight faces (the cross-section of the vajra jewel-pillar is an octagon), with eight ridges complete. Each face is made of a hundred treasures. Each jewel within has a thousand rays of light; each ray of light has eighty-four thousand colors that reflect upon the crystal ground, bright like a billion suns, so that it cannot be examined closely.

[Upon the crystal ground, with golden cords, interwoven and crossed, and with the seven treasures marking the boundaries, all clear and distinct. Within each treasure are five hundred hues of light. That light is like flowers, and resembles stars and moon, suspended in space, forming a platform of light.]

Upon the emerald crystal ground are inlaid narrow golden cords, crossing and interwoven (just as on a marble floor in the world, narrow golden cords divide the crystal ground into one square after another); and the seven treasures form the boundary of each section, neat and distinct. Within each treasure are five hundred hues of light. That light is like flowers, and resembles stars and the moon, suspended in space, forming a platform of light.
[To intermingle] To mix among.

[Pavilions and towers by the thousands, all made of a hundred treasures. On either side of the platform, each has a hundred billion flower banners, with countless musical instruments as adornment. Eight kinds of pure breeze issue from the light, playing these instruments, proclaiming the sounds of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self. This is called the contemplation of water, the second contemplation.]

On the platform of light are pavilions and towers by the thousands, all made of a hundred treasures. On either side of the platform, each has a hundred billion flower banners, to which countless musical instruments hang as adornment. Eight kinds of pure breeze issue from the light, playing these instruments, proclaiming the sounds of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self. This is called the contemplation of water, named the second contemplation.

[Flower banner] A banner-pole adorned with fresh flowers. [Suffering, emptiness, impermanence, non-self] Suffering means that this brief life has three sufferings, eight sufferings, and countless sufferings; suffering is the nature of life. Emptiness means that all dharmas are illusions; the Diamond Sutra says:
“All conditioned appearances are all false and unreal.”
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra says:
“All dharmas are like phantom appearances; the Tathāgata, being in the midst of them, by the power of skillful means is without attachment.”
The Lotus Sutra says:
“The great bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates all dharmas as empty, of real aspect, not inverted, not moving, not regressing, not turning.”

Impermanence means that all dharmas are ceaselessly changing, vanishing in an instant. Non-self means that the body and mind, which are the temporary combination of the five skandhas (form, feeling, perception, formation, consciousness), are not you; your own nature is you. (On self-nature, see
Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathāgata Store
.) [All dharmas] Refers to all the things and phenomena in the boundless universe.

[The three sufferings] The suffering of suffering, the suffering of decay, and the suffering of transience. The suffering of suffering: beings in the world already have a body subject to birth and death, which is suffering enough; added to the pressing of all the manifold sufferings, it is suffering upon suffering, hence the suffering of suffering. The suffering of decay: the suffering felt when a happiness that arises only for a time passes away. The suffering of transience: the suffering of all conditioned things being impermanent, flowing on without rest, and never finding stability. In the realm of desire, all three sufferings are complete; in the realm of form, only the suffering of decay and transience; in the formless realm, only the suffering of transience. [The eight sufferings] First, the suffering of birth, the pain of being born. Second, the suffering of aging, the pain of old age and debility. Third, the suffering of sickness, the pain of illness. Fourth, the suffering of death, the pain of dying. Fifth, the suffering of separation from the beloved. Sixth, the suffering of meeting the hated. Seventh, the suffering of not obtaining what is sought. Eighth, the suffering of the raging of the five aggregates, the functions of the five aggregates being fierce and covering the true nature, so that after death one is reborn again.
[The temporarily combined body and mind are not you] The Complete Enlightenment Sutra says:

“All sentient beings, from beginningless time, have had all manner of inversion, like a deluded person who mistakes the four directions and misplaces them, falsely taking the four great elements as the appearance of a self, and the reflections of the six sense objects as the appearance of a mind. It is like a diseased eye that sees flowers in the sky and a second moon. In the sky there are in reality no flowers; the sick one falsely grasps them. Because of this false grasping, not only is one deluded about the nature of this emptiness, but one is also deluded as to where the real flowers arise. Because of this false existence, one revolves in birth and death; therefore it is called ignorance.”

(Translation: All sentient beings, from beginningless time, with self-nature confused and inverted, give rise to all manner of delusion, mistaking the false for the true — this is ignorance. It is like a person who has lost his bearings and mistakes north for south, east for west, falsely taking the physical body formed of the four great elements of earth, water, fire, and wind as the appearance of a self, and the mind of discrimination that arises from the six senses conditioning on the six objects (the reflections of the six sense objects) as the appearance of a mind. This is like a person with a diseased eye who falsely sees flowers in the sky and a second moon. In reality, there are no flowers in the sky; this is the illusion falsely grasped by the diseased eye, and because of the false grasping, one not only falsely grasps emptiness as real, but also imagines that flowers truly arise from it. Sentient beings, because of their delusion and confusion, falsely take the temporarily manifested body and mind as real and cling to them as a self; therefore they revolve unceasingly in birth and death, and this is called ignorance.)

[The five skandhas] The form aggregate, the feeling aggregate, the perception aggregate, the formation aggregate, and the consciousness aggregate. These five, being accumulated and arisen, are called the “five skandhas”; also, because they can cover a person’s true nature, causing delusion and inversion and the doing of all karma, they are also called the “five aggregates.” Among them, form refers to matter and is called the “dharma of form”; the four aggregates of feeling, perception, formation, and consciousness belong to the mind and are called the “dharma of mind.” These are the five great elements that make up body and mind. Among them, form is the physical body, and the other four (feeling, perception, formation, consciousness) are the mind. [The four great elements] All tangible matter in the world is composed of the four elements of earth, water, fire, and wind, hence they are called “great”: the great earth element, the great water element, the great fire element, and the great wind element. Earth has solidity as its nature, water has moisture as its nature, fire has warmth as its nature, and wind has movement as its nature. [The reflections of the six sense objects] The six sense organs (eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, mind) and the six sense objects (form, sound, smell, taste, touch, dharma) interact, producing a discriminative, clinging, discriminating mind; this discriminating mind is called the reflections of the six sense objects — the phantom reflections produced when the six sense organs condition on the six sense objects. [Flowers in the sky] That is, flowers in the air. “Flower” in the classical text is the same as “flower.”

[When this contemplation is accomplished, contemplate each and every one of them, making them utterly clear and distinct. Whether the eyes are closed or open, do not let them be lost. Except when sleeping, always remember this matter. One who contemplates thus is said to have a rough vision of the ground of the Land of Utmost Bliss. If one attains samādhi, seeing the ground of that land, clear and distinct, it cannot be told in full. This is called the contemplation of the ground, the third contemplation.]

When the contemplation of water is accomplished, contemplate each and every one of them, making them utterly clear and distinct. Whether the eyes are closed or open, do not let them be lost. Except when sleeping, always contemplate this matter. One who contemplates thus is said to have a rough vision of the ground of the Land of Utmost Bliss. If one enters samādhi, seeing the ground of that land (the Western Land of Utmost Bliss), clear and distinct, it cannot be told in full detail. This is called the contemplation of the ground, named the third contemplation.

[The Buddha told Ānanda: You should uphold the Buddha’s words and, for all the multitudes of future ages who wish to escape suffering, speak this method of contemplating the ground. If one contemplates this ground, one removes the offenses of birth and death of eight hundred billion kalpas. At the end of this body and in another rebirth, one will surely be born in the pure land, with a mind without doubt. One who makes this contemplation is called right contemplation; if one contemplates something else, it is called wrong contemplation.]

The Buddha told Ānanda: You should firmly remember my words and, for all the multitudes of future ages who wish to escape suffering, speak this method of contemplating the ground. If one is able to contemplate this ground thus, one removes the offenses of birth and death of eight hundred billion kalpas. After the end of life, one will surely be born in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss, with a mind without the slightest doubt. One who makes this contemplation is called right contemplation. If one contemplates other things, it is called wrong contemplation.

[At the end of this body and in another rebirth] “At the end of this body” means the end of this life; “in another rebirth” means the next life. “At the end of this body and in another rebirth, one will surely be born in the pure land”: after the end of this life, the next life will surely be birth in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss.

blocks.text: Four. The Contemplation of the Jewelled Trees

inline.s: [The Buddha told Ānanda and Vaidehī: When the contemplation of the ground is accomplished, next contemplate the jewelled trees. Contemplate the jewelled trees, one by one. Make the contemplation of a sevenfold row of trees; each tree is eight thousand yojanas high. All these jewelled trees, with flowers and leaves of the seven treasures, are complete in every respect.]

The Buddha told Ānanda and Vaidehī: When the contemplation of the ground is accomplished, the next step is to contemplate the jewelled trees. One who contemplates the jewelled trees should contemplate them one by one. Make the contemplation of a sevenfold row of trees; each tree is eight thousand yojanas high. All these jewelled trees, with flowers (blossoms) and leaves of the seven treasures, are complete in every respect.
[Yojana] A unit for measuring distance in India. There are three kinds, large, medium, and small: a large yojana is about eighty li; a medium yojana about sixty li; a small yojana about forty li.

[Each flower and leaf has the color of a different treasure. From the color of crystal comes forth a golden light; from the color of glass comes forth a red light; from the color of agate comes forth the light of conch-shell; from the color of conch-shell comes forth the light of green pearls. Coral and amber, and all the treasures, serve as reflecting adornments. A splendid net of true pearls covers the trees.]

Each flower and leaf has the color of a different treasure. From the color of crystal comes forth a golden light; from the color of glass comes forth a red light; from the color of agate comes forth the light of conch-shell; from the color of conch-shell comes forth the light of green pearls. Coral and amber and all the manifold treasures reflect and adorn one another. A splendid net of true pearls spreads and covers the trees.
[Conch-shell (
chē qú
)] One of the seven treasures. According to the record in The Expanded Compendium of Materia Medica, fascicle forty-six, conch-shell is a great clam of the sea (
gé

), whose shell has markings like ridges, like the ruts of a wheel (the tracks a wheel leaves on the ground); the inside of the shell is white as jade, so it is often mistaken for jade of the stone class. In later times, objects made of white coral and shells are mostly taken for conch-shell. [The seven treasures] Gold, silver, crystal, glass, conch-shell, red pearls, and agate.

[Upon each tree are seven nets. Between each net are five hundred billion wondrous flower palaces, like the palace of Brahmā. Heavenly youths abide naturally within. Each youth wears five hundred billion of the Śakra-prajṅā jewel of the mani, as a necklace. These mani lights shine a hundred yojanas, like a hundred billion suns and moons combined, beyond naming. The manifold treasures interweave, colors the most supreme among colors.]

Upon each tree are seven nets. Between each net are five hundred billion wondrous flower palaces, like the palace of Brahmā. Heavenly youths naturally dwell within them. Each youth wears a necklace made of the mani jewels of Śakra the Indra of five hundred billion. These mani lights shine a hundred yojanas, like a hundred billion suns and moons combined, bright and wondrous, beyond telling. The manifold treasures interweave, all with the most beautiful colors. All these jewelled trees, row after row arranged neatly, leaf after leaf spaced in order.
[The Śakra-prajñā mani jewel] “Śakra-prajñā” is translated “held by Indra,” meaning “the possession of Indra (ruler of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven).” “Mani jewel” is the wish-fulfilling jewel.

[These jewelled trees, row after row corresponding, leaf after leaf in succession. Among the manifold leaves grow all manner of wondrous flowers, upon which there are naturally the fruits of the seven treasures. Each leaf, in length and breadth, is exactly twenty-five yojanas. These leaves have a thousand colors and a hundred designs, like the heavenly necklace. There are many wondrous flowers, of the Jambūnada gold color, like revolving fire-wheels, turning among the leaves. There spring up manifold fruits, like the vase of Indra, with great light, transforming into banners and canopies and countless jewelled parasols.]

All these jewelled trees, row after row arranged neatly, leaf after leaf spaced in order. Among the manifold leaves grow all manner of wondrous flowers, upon which there are naturally the fruits of the seven treasures. Each leaf, in length and breadth, is exactly twenty-five yojanas. These leaves have a thousand colors and a hundred designs, like the necklace of heavenly beings. There are many wondrous flowers, of the Jambūnada gold color, like revolving fire-wheels, turning among the leaves. There spring up many fruits, like the vase of Indra, sending forth great light, transforming into banners and canopies and countless jewelled parasols.

[Jambūnada gold] Its color is red and yellow, with a flame-like purple aura, the noblest of all golds. [The vase of Indra] The precious vase of Indra, lord of the heavens, from which all things needed naturally spring forth.

[In these jewelled parasols are reflected all the Buddha-acts of the three-thousand-great-thousand world, and the Buddha-lands of the ten directions also appear within. Having seen these trees, one should also contemplate them one by one in succession, seeing the trunks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits of the trees, all made clear and distinct. This is called the contemplation of trees, the fourth contemplation.]

In these jewelled parasols are reflected all the Buddha-acts of the three-thousand-great-thousand world, and the Buddha-lands of the ten directions also appear within them. Having seen these trees, one should also contemplate them one by one in succession, seeing the trunks, branches, leaves, flowers (blossoms), and fruits of the trees, all made clear and distinct (each and every one clear and distinct). This is called the contemplation of trees, named the fourth contemplation.

[The three-thousand-great-thousand world] That is, a great chiliocosm, the region which one Buddha teaches, that is, one Buddha-lands. A Mount Sumeru plus the four great continents is called a small world. A thousand small worlds make a “small thousand world”; a thousand small thousand worlds make a “middle thousand world”; a thousand middle thousand worlds make a “great thousand world.” Because it is called a thousand three times, a great thousand world is also called the “three-thousand-great-thousand world.” [Mount Sumeru] Translated as “wondrously high mountain,” it is the center of a small world. This mountain is made of gold, silver, crystal, and crystal the four treasures; no mountains can rival its height, and it is king of mountains. [The four great continents] Around Mount Sumeru are four great continents: the eastern is called Purvavideha, the southern is called Jambudvipa (the world in which we live is on this continent), the western is called Godaniya, and the northern is called Uttarakuru.

blocks.text: Five. The Contemplation of the Pools

inline.s: [Next one should contemplate water. One who wishes to contemplate water: the Land of Utmost Bliss has eight pools of water. Each pool is made of the seven treasures. These treasures, being soft, arise from the king of wish-fulfilling jewels. They divide into fourteen streams; each stream has the color of the seven treasures. Gold is the channel, and beneath the channel are variegated vajras as the sand of the bottom. In each pool are six billion lotus flowers of the seven treasures; each lotus is perfectly round, exactly twelve yojanas in diameter.]

Next, one should contemplate water. One who wishes to contemplate water: the Land of Utmost Bliss has eight pools of water. Each pool is transformed from the seven treasures. These treasures, being soft, arise from the king of wish-fulfilling jewels. The pools divide into fourteen streams; each stream has the color of the seven treasures. Gold is the channel, and beneath the channel are variegated vajras as the sand of the bottom. In each stream are six billion lotus flowers of the seven treasures. Each lotus is perfectly round (rather than elliptical or any other imperfect shape), and its diameter is twelve yojanas.
[Wish-fulfilling jewel] A jewel which, being sought, fulfills one’s wishes. [King of wish-fulfilling jewels] The most excellent among wish-fulfilling jewels, hence called king.

[The mani water flows among the flowers and goes up and down the trees; its sound is subtle, proclaiming the various perfections of ‘suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self,’ and again there are those who praise the auspicious marks of the Buddhas.]

The wish-fulfilling water (mani water) of the seven-jewel pools flows among the flowers and goes up and down along the trees; its sound is subtle and wondrous, proclaiming the various wondrous dharmas that carry beings to the other shore of nirvāṇa, such as ‘suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self,’ and there are also subtle and wondrous sounds praising the auspicious marks of the Buddhas.

[Mani water] Wish-fulfilling water. Here “mani” means “wish-fulfilling.” For example, the mani jewel, that is, the wish-fulfilling jewel, from which treasures, clothes, food, and drink and all manner of things that are wanted are produced, causing all beings to obtain their wishes.
The Amita Assembly of the Immeasurable Life Sūtra says:

“When the Immeasurably Pure Buddha and the various bodhisattvas and arhats wish to bathe, each enters the seven-jewel pool to bathe. The bodhisattvas and arhats, wishing the water to cover the feet, the water covers the feet. Wishing the water to reach the knees, the water reaches the knees. Wishing the water to reach the waist, the water reaches the waist. Wishing the water to reach the armpits, the water reaches the armpits. Wishing the water to reach the neck, the water reaches the neck. Wishing the water to pour over the body, the water pours over the body. Wishing the water to return again to its former state, the water returns to its former state. As one wishes freely, so one delights.”
Therefore, the water in the seven-jewel pools is wish-fulfilling water. [To follow] Here it means to go along, to follow. For example, in the History of the Later Han,

the Biographies of Yuan Shao and Liu Biao says: “Yuan Shao then followed the mountain and went north.” (Translation: Yuan Shao then went north along the mountain.) [Pāramitā] To reach the other shore, that is, from this shore of the realm of delusion in birth and death to the other shore of the liberation of nirvāṇa.

[Suffering, emptiness, impermanence, non-self] Suffering means that this brief life has the three sufferings, the eight sufferings, and countless sufferings. Emptiness is dependent origination and emptiness of intrinsic nature: dependent origination means that worldly dharmas arise from the combination of conditions; emptiness of intrinsic nature means that the dharmas arising from the combination of conditions have a nature originally empty, without a real self-substance. Impermanence is the impermanence of all conditioned things, meaning that worldly dharmas are all ceaselessly changing, arising and ceasing without end, with no eternally abiding unchanging entity. Non-self is the selflessness of all dharmas: worldly birth and death and all dharmas come into being through the combination of causes and conditions, false and unreal, without a self-substance. [The three sufferings] The suffering of suffering, the suffering of decay, and the suffering of transience. The suffering of suffering: beings in the world already have a body subject to birth and death, which is suffering enough; added to the pressing of the manifold sufferings, it is suffering upon suffering, hence the suffering of suffering. The suffering of decay: the suffering felt when a happiness that appears only for a time passes away. The suffering of transience: the suffering of all conditioned things being impermanent, flowing on without rest, and never finding stability. [The eight sufferings] First, the suffering of birth, the pain of being born. Second, the suffering of aging, the pain of old age and debility. Third, the suffering of sickness, the pain of illness. Fourth, the suffering of death, the pain of dying. Fifth, the suffering of separation from the beloved. Sixth, the suffering of meeting those one hates. Seventh, the suffering of not obtaining what is sought. Eighth, the suffering of the raging of the five aggregates: the functions of the five aggregates (skandhas) being fierce and covering the true nature.

[From the king of wish-fulfilling jewels springs forth a golden and subtle light. That light transforms into birds of a hundred jewel colors, singing in harmony with sweet and elegant tones, ever praising ‘recalling the Buddha, recalling the Dharma, recalling the sangha.’ This is called the contemplation of the water of eight qualities, the fifth contemplation.]

From the king of wish-fulfilling jewels of the seven-jewel pools springs forth a golden and subtle light. That light transforms into birds of a hundred jewel colors, singing in harmony with one another (harmonious song), their tones sorrowful and elegant (sweet and elegant), ever praising ‘recalling the Buddha, recalling the Dharma, recalling the sangha.’ What is above is called the contemplation of the water of eight qualities, named the fifth contemplation.
[A hundred jewel colors] Their magnificent colors are like a hundred treasures blended together.

blocks.text: Six. The Comprehensive Contemplation

inline.s: [In the land of manifold treasures, upon each and every region are five hundred billion jewel towers. Within these pavilions and towers are countless heavenly beings performing heavenly music. Again there are musical instruments, suspended in space, like heavenly jewel banners, sounding without being struck. Among these manifold sounds, all speak of recalling the Buddha, recalling the Dharma, and recalling the bhikṣu sangha. When this contemplation is accomplished, it is called a rough vision of the jewelled trees, jewelled ground, and jewelled pools of the Land of Utmost Bliss. This is the comprehensive contemplation, the sixth contemplation.]

In the land constituted of manifold treasures, upon each and every region are five hundred billion jewel towers. Within these pavilions and towers are countless heavenly beings performing the music and dance of heaven. Again there are musical instruments, suspended in space, like heavenly jewel banners, sounding without being struck. Among these manifold sounds, all speak of recalling the Buddha, recalling the Dharma, and recalling the bhikṣu sangha. When this contemplation is accomplished, it is called a rough vision of the jewelled trees, jewelled ground, and jewelled pools of the Land of Utmost Bliss. It is called the comprehensive contemplation, named the sixth contemplation.
[Music and dance (
jì
)] Music and dance.

[If one sees this, one removes the most weighty evil karma of countless billions of kalpas, and after the end of life, one will surely be born in that land. One who makes this contemplation is called right contemplation; if one contemplates something else, it is called wrong contemplation.]

If one accomplishes this contemplation, one removes the most weighty evil karma of countless billions of kalpas, and after the end of life, one will surely be born in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss. One who contemplates thus is called right contemplation; if one contemplates other things, it is called wrong contemplation.

blocks.text: Seven. The Contemplation of the Lotus Throne

inline.s: [The Buddha told Ānanda and Vaidehī: Listen! Listen! Think on it well! I shall for you, one by one, explain the method that removes suffering. You should remember and uphold it, and for the many, explain it one by one.]

The Buddha told Ānanda and Vaidehī: Listen! Listen! Think on it well! I shall for you, one by one, explain the method that removes suffering. You should remember and uphold it, and for the many, explain it one by one.

[When he had spoken these words, the Buddha of Immeasurable Life stood in the air, and Avalokitesvara and Mahasthamaprapta, these two great beings, attended on his left and right. Their light blazed so brightly that it could not be fully beheld, and a hundred thousand jambu river gold hues could not be compared to it.]

When these words had been spoken, the Buddha of Immeasurable Life stood in the air, and the two great beings Avalokitesvara and Mahasthamaprapta attended on his left and right. Their light blazed so brightly that one could not look upon it closely, and a hundred thousand jambu river gold hues could not compare with it at all.

[Then Vaidehī, having seen the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, bowed at his feet in reverence and said to the Buddha: ‘World-Honored One, it is by the Buddha’s power that I have now been able to see the Buddha of Immeasurable Life and the two bodhisattvas. How should the beings of the future contemplate the Buddha of Immeasurable Life and the two bodhisattvas?’]

At that time, having seen the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, Vaidehī bowed at his feet in reverence and said to the Buddha: ‘World-Honored One, it is by the Buddha’s power that I have now come to see the Buddha of Immeasurable Life and the two bodhisattvas. By what means can the beings of the future come to see the Buddha of Immeasurable Life and the two bodhisattvas?’

[The Buddha said to Vaidehī: Those who wish to contemplate that Buddha should form this mental image: upon the ground of the seven treasures, visualize a lotus flower, and let each and every petal of that lotus bear a hundred jewel hues, with eighty-four thousand veins like heavenly paintings. Each and every vein has eighty-four thousand rays of light, perfectly distinct, and all should be made visible. Even the smallest petal is two hundred and fifty yojanas in length and breadth.]

The Buddha said to Vaidehī: Those who wish to see the Buddha of Immeasurable Life and the two bodhisattvas should contemplate in this way: upon the ground of the seven treasures, visualize a lotus flower, and let each and every petal of that lotus bear a hundred jewel hues, with eighty-four thousand veins like wondrous paintings in the heavens. Each and every vein has eighty-four thousand rays of light, perfectly distinct, and all should be contemplated clearly. Even the smallest petal is two hundred and fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
