[Seeing the Buddha of Immeasurable Life and the two bodhisattvas] The present passage on the contemplation of the lotus throne, together with the contemplations of the sacred image, the Buddha’s body, Avalokitesvara, and Mahasthamaprapta that follow, sets forth precisely how to see the Buddha of Immeasurable Life and the two bodhisattvas.

[Such a lotus flower has eighty-four thousand great petals. Between each and every petal are a hundred billion kings of mani pearls as adornment. Each and every mani pearl emits a thousand rays of light. That light forms a canopy made of the seven treasures, covering the ground entirely. The Sakrabhilagna mani jewel forms its dais. This lotus dais is adorned with eighty thousand adamantine kimshuka jewels, Brahma mani jewels, and nets of wonderful pearls.]

This lotus flower has eighty-four thousand great petals. Between each and every petal are a hundred billion kings of mani pearls as adornment. Each and every mani pearl emits a thousand rays of light. That light forms a canopy made of the seven treasures, covering the whole ground. The wish-fulfilling jewel of Sakra forms the flower dais. This lotus dais is adorned with eighty thousand adamantine red jewels, Brahma mani jewels, and nets of wonderful pearls.
[Kimshuka] The name of a gem; rendered in Chinese as ‘red jewel’. [Brahma mani jewel] The wish-fulfilling pearl of the great Brahma king.

[Upon that dais there naturally appear four jewelled standards. Each and every jewelled standard is as vast as a hundred thousand million billion Mount Sumerus. The jewelled canopies upon the standards are like the palace of the Yama Heaven, and there are again five hundred billion subtle and wonderful pearls as adornment. Each and every pearl has eighty-four thousand rays of light, and each and every ray produces eighty-four thousand different hues of gold. Each and every golden hue pervades that jewelled land, transforming everywhere and assuming various forms: sometimes an adamantine dais, sometimes a pearl net, sometimes clouds of manifold flowers, appearing at will in the ten directions and performing the Buddha’s work. This is the contemplation of the lotus throne, called the seventh contemplation.]

Upon the lotus dais there naturally appear four jewelled standards. Each and every jewelled standard is as vast as a hundred thousand million billion Mount Sumerus. The jewelled canopies upon the standards are like the palace of the Yama Heaven, and there are again five hundred billion subtle and wonderful pearls as adornment. Each and every pearl has eighty-four thousand rays of light, and each and every ray has eighty-four thousand different hues of gold. Each and every golden hue illumines that jewelled land, transforming everywhere and assuming various forms: sometimes an adamantine dais, sometimes a pearl net, sometimes clouds of manifold flowers, appearing at will in the ten directions and performing the Buddha’s work. The above is called the contemplation of the lotus throne, named the seventh contemplation.

[The Buddha said to Ānanda: This wonderful flower was brought into being by the power of the vows of the monk Dharmakara in a former life. If one wishes to be mindful of that Buddha, one should first form this contemplation of the wonderful lotus throne. When making this contemplation, one must not contemplate anything else. All should be contemplated one by one: each and every petal, each and every pearl, each and every ray of light, each and every dais, each and every standard should be made clear and distinct, as when one sees one’s own face in a mirror. When this contemplation is accomplished, one erases the offenses of birth and death of five hundred billion kalpas and will certainly be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. One who makes this contemplation is called right contemplation; if one contemplates something else, it is called wrong contemplation.]

The Buddha told Ānanda: This wonderful lotus throne was brought into being by the power of the original vows of the monk Dharmakara. If one wishes to see the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, one should first form this contemplation of the wonderful lotus throne. When making this contemplation, one must not contemplate other things. Every detail of the wonderful lotus throne should be contemplated one by one — each and every petal, each and every pearl, each and every ray of light, each and every dais, each and every standard — all made clear and distinct, as when one sees one’s own face in a mirror. One who accomplishes this contemplation erases the offenses of birth and death of five hundred billion kalpas and will certainly be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. One who makes this contemplation is called right contemplation; if one contemplates other things, it is called wrong contemplation.
[The monk Dharmakara] This is the name of Amitābha Buddha (the Buddha of Immeasurable Life) during his causal stage, when he left home and cultivated the bodhisattva path.

blocks.text: Eight. The Contemplation of the Sacred Image

inline.s: [The Buddha said to Ānanda and Vaidehī: When you have seen this, next you should contemplate the Buddha. Why is this? All Buddhas, the Tathagatas, are the Dharma-realm body, and they enter everywhere into the minds of all sentient beings. Therefore, when you contemplate the Buddha in your minds, this mind is itself the thirty-two marks and the eighty minor marks. This mind creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha. The ocean of the Buddhas’ perfect and universal knowledge arises from mental contemplation. Therefore, with one mind, wholeheartedly recollect and clearly contemplate that Buddha — the Tathagata, the Arhat, the Rightly and Universally Enlightened One.]

The Buddha told Ānanda and Vaidehī: After the contemplation of the wonderful lotus throne, the next step is to contemplate Amitābha Buddha (the Buddha of Immeasurable Life). Why is this? All Buddhas, the Tathagatas, are the Dharma-realm body, and they enter everywhere into the minds of all sentient beings. Therefore, when you contemplate Amitābha Buddha in your minds, this mind is itself the thirty-two marks and the eighty minor marks. This mind creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha. The Buddhas, numerous as the waters of the great ocean, are all brought to accomplishment by single-mindedly contemplating Amitābha Buddha (by single-mindedly recollecting and clearly contemplating that Buddha). Therefore, one should single-mindedly recollect and clearly contemplate Amitābha Buddha.

[The Dharma-realm body] The body that pervades the Dharma realm, that is, the Dharma body (dharmakāya) among the Buddha’s three bodies. [The three bodies] The Dharma body, the reward body, and the response body. 1. The Dharma body, also called the body of self-nature or the body of Dharma-nature: the true nature that is everlasting and unchanging and is inherent in everyone. It is only that we sentient beings are deluded, so it does not appear, while the Buddha is enlightened and has realized it. 2. The reward body: the body produced by the Buddha’s wisdom and merit, which is distinguished as the reward body for his own enjoyment and the reward body for others’ enjoyment. The reward body for his own enjoyment is the body with which the Buddha himself enjoys the bliss of inner realization; the reward body for others’ enjoyment is the body manifested by the Buddha to teach the bodhisattvas of the ten stages. 3. The response body, also called the responsive transformation body or the transformation body: the Buddha body manifested in response to the particular capacities of sentient beings.

[The thirty-two marks] Also called the thirty-two marks of the great man, or the thirty-two marks of a great being: 1. level and even soles; 2. a thousand-spoked wheel on each sole; 3. slender and long fingers; 4. soft and tender hands and feet; 5. webbed hands and feet; 6. full and rounded heels; 7. high and well-formed insteps; 8. the calves (
shuàn

the calf of the leg) like a deer king’s; 9. hands reaching past the knees; 10. the male organ drawn in like a horse’s; 11. the body equal in height and breadth; 12. dark blue pores; 13. body hair curling upward; 14. a golden body; 15. a constant light of one fathom; 16. fine and smooth skin; 17. the seven places full and level; 18. full armpits; 19. a body like a lion’s; 20. an upright and well-proportioned body; 21. full and rounded shoulders; 22. forty teeth; 23. white, even, and close-set teeth; 24. four white and pure canine teeth; 25. jawbones (the palate bones that hold the teeth) like a lion’s; 26. the finest flavor obtained by the saliva in the throat; 27. a broad and long tongue; 28. a pure and far-carrying Brahma voice; 29. dark blue eyes; 30. eyelashes like a bull king’s; 31. a white curl between the eyebrows; 32. a fleshy mound upon the crown. [Dark blue (
gàn
) blue] A color of black shot through with red.

[The eighty minor marks] Namely: an invisible crown; a high nose with unseen nostrils; eyebrows like the new moon; long pendulous earlobes; a body firm and solid as Narayana’s; joints like hooked chains; the body turning about at once like an elephant king; when walking, the feet four inches above the ground yet leaving a print; nails the color of red copper, thin and lustrous; knee bones firm and beautifully round; a clean body; a soft body; a body that is not bent; round and slender fingers; the lines of the fingers concealed; veins deep and unseen; ankles not protruding; a lustrous body; a body that holds itself up without slouching; a body full and complete; perfect bearing and demeanor; bearing and demeanor complete and full; abiding securely so that none can move him; majesty overawing all; all beings rejoicing at the sight of him; a face neither long nor large; upright features with an unchanging countenance; a face and eyes full and complete; lips the color of the bimba fruit; a voice deep and far-reaching; a navel deep and beautifully round; body hair curling to the right; hands and feet full and complete; hands and feet compliant at will; the lines of the hands bright and straight; the lines of the hands long; the lines of the hands unbroken; all beings of evil mind becoming gentle and joyful on seeing him; a broad and exceedingly beautiful face; a face pure and full like the moon; speaking gently and joyfully in accordance with beings’ minds; fragrance issuing from his pores; supreme fragrance issuing from his mouth; a bearing like a lion’s; advancing and halting like an elephant king; walking like a goose king; a head like a madana fruit; a voice complete in all its tones; four teeth white and sharp; a tongue red in color; a thin tongue; body hair red in color; body hair soft and clean; eyes broad and long; possessing the marks of the gate of death; hands and feet red and white like a lotus flower; a navel that does not protrude; a belly that does not bulge; a slender belly; a body that does not lean or move; a body of weight; a large body; a tall body; hands and feet soft, clean, smooth, and lustrous; light extending one fathom on all four sides; the light shining as he walks; looking upon all beings with equality; not slighting any being; not adding to or diminishing the sounds of beings; teaching the Dharma without attachment; teaching the Dharma in accordance with the speech of beings; a voice that responds to beings; teaching the Dharma in sequence according to causes and conditions; all beings unable to exhaust the contemplation of his marks; contemplation that is never satiated; hair long and beautiful; hair not disordered; hair curling beautifully; hair the color of dark blue pearls; hands and feet as the marks of virtue.

[The ocean of the Buddhas’ perfect and universal knowledge arises from mental contemplation] The Buddhas, numerous as the waters of the great ocean, are all brought to accomplishment by single-mindedly contemplating Amitābha Buddha (by single-mindedly recollecting and clearly contemplating that Buddha). [Perfect and universal knowledge] Perfect and universal knowledge means truly and universally knowing all dharmas. This is one of the Buddha’s ten epithets. [The Buddha’s ten epithets] The Buddha has ten honored titles: 1. Tathagata, one who comes by the way of Suchness to accomplish perfect enlightenment; 2. Worthy of Offerings, one worthy of the offerings of gods and humans; 3. Rightly and Universally Enlightened One, one who truly and universally knows all dharmas; 4. Perfect in Wisdom and Practice, one complete in the three insights — the insight into past lives, the divine eye, and the extinction of outflows — and in the five practices — the holy practice, the Brahma practice, the heavenly practice, the infant practice, and the practice of sickness; 5. Well-Gone, one who freely departs well and enters nirvāṇa; 6. Knower of the World, one able to understand the affairs and principles of all worlds; 7. Unsurpassed One, the being who is supreme and without superior; 8. Tamer of Men, the great being who can tame and guide others onto the right path; 9. Teacher of Gods and Men, the Buddha being the guide of all gods and humans; 10. Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Buddha being the one honored in common by all the world. [Tathagata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha] Tathagata is rendered in Chinese as ‘Thus Come One’. Arhat is rendered as ‘Worthy of Offerings’. Samyaksambuddha is rendered as ‘Rightly and Universally Enlightened One’. These are the first three of the Buddha’s ten epithets.

[Those who contemplate that Buddha should first contemplate his image. Whether the eyes are closed or open, one sees a jewelled image, the color of jambu river gold, seated upon that lotus. When the image is seated, the mind’s eye opens, and one sees clearly and distinctly the seven treasures adorning the Land of Ultimate Bliss: jewelled ground, jewelled pools, and rows of jewelled trees, with celestial jewelled canopies spread over the trees, and nets of many treasures filling the sky. Seeing such things, one should make them exceedingly clear, as if looking at something in the palm of one’s hand.]

Those who contemplate Amitābha Buddha should first contemplate the Buddha’s image. Whether the eyes are closed or open, one sees a jewelled image, the color of jambu river gold, seated upon that lotus throne. When the image is seated upon the lotus throne, the practitioner’s mind’s eye opens, and he sees clearly and distinctly the seven treasures adorning the Land of Ultimate Bliss: jewelled ground, jewelled pools, and rows of jewelled trees, with celestial jewelled canopies spread over the trees, and nets of many treasures filling the sky. When one sees such things, one must make them exceedingly clear, as if looking at something in the palm of one’s hand.

[Having seen this, one should further form a great lotus flower to the left of the Buddha, identical in every way to the lotus flower described above. Then form another great lotus flower to the right of the Buddha. Visualize an image of Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva seated upon the left lotus throne, also emitting golden light, no different from what was described above. Then visualize an image of Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva seated upon the right lotus throne.]

Having seen the above, one should further visualize a great lotus throne to the left of Amitābha Buddha, exactly like the lotus throne contemplated above, without the slightest difference. There is also a great lotus throne to the right of Amitābha Buddha. Visualize the image of Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva seated upon the left lotus throne, also emitting golden light, entirely the same as the light described above. Then visualize the image of Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva seated upon the right lotus throne.

[When this contemplation is accomplished, the images of the Buddha and the bodhisattvas all emit light. That light is golden in color and illumines all the jewelled trees. Beneath each and every tree there are also three lotus flowers, and upon each and every lotus flower there is an image of one Buddha and two bodhisattvas, filling that land everywhere. When this contemplation is accomplished, the practitioner hears the streams of water, the light, and all the jewelled trees, the ducks, the geese, and the mandarin ducks all proclaiming the wonderful Dharma. Whether entering samādhi or rising from it, he constantly hears the wonderful Dharma.]

When this contemplation is accomplished, the images of the Buddha and the bodhisattvas all emit light. That light is golden in color and illumines all the jewelled trees. Beneath each and every tree there are also three lotus thrones, and upon each and every lotus throne there is an image of one Buddha and two bodhisattvas, filling that land everywhere. When this contemplation is accomplished, the practitioner hears the streams of water, the light, and all the jewelled trees, ducks, geese, and mandarin ducks all proclaiming the wonderful Dharma. Whether entering samādhi or rising from it, he always hears the wonderful Dharma.

[What the practitioner hears, at the time of rising from samādhi, he remembers and holds without letting go, and makes it accord with the sutras. If it does not accord, it is called a deluded thought. If it does accord, it is called a rough vision of the Land of Ultimate Bliss. This is the contemplation of the image, named the eighth contemplation. One who makes this contemplation removes the offenses of birth and death of immeasurable billions of kalpas, and in this present body attains the samādhi of Buddha-recitation.]

The wonderful Dharma heard by the practitioner in samādhi, at the time of rising from samādhi he also remembers and holds without letting go, and makes it accord with the sutra text (the sutras). If it does not accord, it is called a deluded thought. If it accords with the sutra text, it is called a rough vision of the Land of Ultimate Bliss. The above is called the contemplation of the image, named the eighth contemplation. One who makes this contemplation removes the offenses of birth and death of immeasurable billions of kalpas, and in this present body attains the samādhi of Buddha-recitation.
[Sutra] Here it means the text of the scriptures. The Dasheng Yizhang says:
“In the Shata Shastra, the scripture text is called xiudulu
(sutra)

blocks.text: Nine. The Contemplation of the Buddha’s Body

inline.s: [The Buddha said to Ānanda and Vaidehī: When this contemplation is accomplished, next you should further contemplate the bodily marks and light of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life.]

The Buddha told Ānanda and Vaidehī: When the contemplation of the images of the three holy ones is accomplished, the next step is to contemplate the bodily marks and light of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life.

[Ānanda, you should know that the body of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life is the color of the jambu river gold of a hundred thousand million Yama heavens. The Buddha’s body is six hundred thousand billion nayutas of Ganges sands yojanas in height. The white curl between his eyebrows curls to the right and revolves, like five Mount Sumerus.]

Ānanda, you should know that the body of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life is the color of the jambu river gold of a hundred thousand million Yama heavens. The Buddha’s body is six hundred thousand billion nayutas of Ganges sands yojanas in height. The white curl between his eyebrows curls to the right and revolves, as great as five Mount Sumerus.

[The Buddha’s eyes are pure like the waters of the four great seas, clear and distinct. From all the pores of his body there streams forth light, like Mount Sumeru. The Buddha’s halo is like a hundred billion three-thousand great thousand worlds. Within the halo are a million billion nayutas of Ganges sands transformation Buddhas. Each and every transformation Buddha likewise has many countless transformation bodhisattvas as attendants.]

The Buddha’s eyes are pure like the waters of the four great seas, clear and distinct. From all the pores of his body there streams forth light, as mighty as Mount Sumeru. The halo of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life is as vast and boundless as a hundred billion three-thousand great thousand worlds. Within the halo are a million billion nayutas of Ganges sands transformation Buddhas. Each and every transformation Buddha likewise has many countless transformation bodhisattvas as attendants.

[The Buddha of Immeasurable Life has eighty-four thousand marks. Within each and every mark are eighty-four thousand secondary marks. Within each and every secondary mark are again eighty-four thousand rays of light. Each and every ray of light illumines everywhere the Buddha-reciting beings of the ten directions, gathering them in and never forsaking them. His light, marks, and secondary marks, together with the transformation Buddhas, cannot be fully described. One should simply recollect and visualize them, causing the mind to see them clearly.]

The Buddha of Immeasurable Life has eighty-four thousand marks. Within each and every mark are eighty-four thousand secondary marks that follow upon that form. Within each and every secondary mark are again eighty-four thousand rays of light. Each and every ray of light illumines everywhere the Buddha-reciting beings of the ten directions, gathering them in and never forsaking them. His light, marks, and secondary marks, together with the transformation Buddhas, cannot be described in detail. One should simply recollect and visualize them, causing the mind to see them clearly.

[One who sees this matter sees all the Buddhas of the ten directions. Because one sees the Buddhas, it is called the samādhi of Buddha-recitation. One who makes this contemplation is said to contemplate the bodies of all Buddhas. Because one contemplates the Buddha’s body, one also sees the Buddha’s mind. The mind of all Buddhas is great compassion. With objectless compassion, they gather in all sentient beings.]

One who sees this matter sees all the Buddhas of the ten directions. Because one sees the Buddhas, it is called the samādhi of Buddha-recitation. One who makes this contemplation is said to contemplate the bodies of all Buddhas. Because one contemplates the Buddha’s body, one also sees the Buddha’s mind. The mind of all Buddhas is great compassion. With objectless compassion, they gather in all sentient beings.

[One who makes this contemplation, when he casts off this body and passes to another life, is born before the Buddhas and attains the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas. Therefore, the wise should gather in their minds and clearly contemplate the Buddha of Immeasurable Life. One who contemplates the Buddha of Immeasurable Life should enter by way of one mark and secondary mark. Simply contemplate the white curl between the eyebrows, making it exceedingly clear. One who sees the mark of the white curl between the eyebrows will naturally see the eighty-four thousand marks and secondary marks.]

One who accomplishes this contemplation, after the end of this life, is born before the Buddhas and attains the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas. Therefore, the wise should gather in their minds and clearly contemplate the Buddha of Immeasurable Life. One who contemplates the Buddha of Immeasurable Life should begin with the contemplation of one mark and secondary mark. Simply contemplate the white curl between the Buddha’s eyebrows, making it exceedingly clear. One who sees the mark of the white curl between the eyebrows will naturally see the Buddha’s eighty-four thousand marks and secondary marks.

[One who sees the Buddha of Immeasurable Life sees all the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions. Because one sees the immeasurable Buddhas, the Buddhas appear before one and bestow a prediction. This is the universal contemplation of all bodily marks, called the ninth contemplation. One who makes this contemplation is called right contemplation. If one contemplates something else, it is called wrong contemplation.]

One who sees the Buddha of Immeasurable Life sees all the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions. Because one sees the immeasurable Buddhas, the Buddhas appear before one and bestow a prediction. This is the universal contemplation of all bodily marks, named the ninth contemplation. One who makes this contemplation is called right contemplation. If one contemplates other things, it is called wrong contemplation.

blocks.text: Ten. The Contemplation of Avalokitesvara

inline.s: [The Buddha said to Ānanda and Vaidehī: When you have seen the Buddha of Immeasurable Life clearly and distinctly, next you should also contemplate Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva.]
The Buddha told Ānanda and Vaidehī: When you have seen the Buddha of Immeasurable Life clearly and distinctly, you should next contemplate Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva.

[This bodhisattva is eighty billion nayutas of Ganges sands yojanas in height, his body the color of purple-gold, with a fleshy mound upon his crown and a halo upon his crown, each of its faces a hundred thousand yojanas across. Within his halo are five hundred transformation Buddhas like Śākyamuni. Each and every transformation Buddha has five hundred transformation bodhisattvas and immeasurable gods as attendants. In the light of his entire body, all the bodily forms of the beings of the five paths appear.]

This bodhisattva is eighty billion nayutas of Ganges sands yojanas in height, his body the color of purple-gold, with a fleshy mound upon his crown and a halo upon his crown, each of its faces a hundred thousand yojanas across. Within his halo are five hundred transformation Buddhas like Śākyamuni. Each and every transformation Buddha has five hundred transformation bodhisattvas and immeasurable gods as attendants. In the light of his entire body, the bodily forms of all the beings of the five paths appear.
[The fleshy mound (
jì

)] A mound of flesh rising upon the crown like a topknot (a knot of hair coiled upon the top or the back of the head), hence it is called the fleshy mound. [In the light of his entire body] This is the bodhisattva’s bodily light. [The five paths] These are the places where sentient beings come and go, hence they are called ‘paths’. There are five: 1. the hell path; 2. the hungry ghost path; 3. the animal path; 4. the human path; 5. the heavenly path.

[Upon his crown is the wonderful Sakrabhilagna mani jewel, forming a heavenly crown. Within that heavenly crown there is a standing transformation Buddha, twenty-five yojanas in height. Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva’s face is the color of jambu river gold. The mark of the white curl between his eyebrows is complete in the seven jewel hues and streams forth eighty-four thousand kinds of light. Within each and every light are immeasurable, countless hundreds of thousands of transformation Buddhas, and each and every transformation Buddha has countless transformation bodhisattvas as attendants, manifesting transformations freely and filling the ten directions.]

Upon his crown, the wonderful wish-fulfilling jewel of Sakra forms a heavenly crown. Within that heavenly crown there is a standing transformation Buddha, twenty-five yojanas in height. Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva’s face is the color of jambu river gold. The mark of the white curl between his eyebrows is complete in the seven jewel hues and streams forth eighty-four thousand kinds of light. Within each and every kind of light are immeasurable, countless hundreds of thousands of transformation Buddhas, and each and every transformation Buddha has countless transformation bodhisattvas as attendants, manifesting transformations freely and filling the ten directions.

[His arms are the color of the red lotus flower, and eighty billion subtle and wonderful rays of light form his necklace, within which all manner of adornments appear everywhere. The palms of his hands are the color of five hundred billion mingled lotus flowers. From the tips of the ten fingers of his hands, each and every fingertip has eighty-four thousand paintings, like the patterns of a seal; each and every painting has eighty-four thousand colors, and each and every color has eighty-four thousand rays of light. That light is soft and gentle, illumining all things everywhere, and with these jewel hands he receives and guides sentient beings.]

His arms are the color of the red lotus flower, and eighty billion subtle and wonderful rays of light form his necklace, within which all manner of adornments appear everywhere. The palms of his hands are the color of five hundred billion mingled lotus flowers. From the tips of the ten fingers of his hands, each and every fingertip has eighty-four thousand paintings, like the patterns printed upon the fingertips; each and every painting has eighty-four thousand colors, and each and every color has eighty-four thousand rays of light. That light is soft and gentle, illumining all things everywhere, and with these jewel hands he receives and guides sentient beings.

[When he lifts his foot, beneath his foot is the mark of a thousand-spoked wheel, which naturally transforms into five hundred billion light platforms. When he sets his foot down, adamantine mani flowers scatter everywhere, leaving nothing uncovered. His remaining bodily marks are complete in all their secondary marks, no different from a Buddha’s. Only the fleshy mound upon his crown and the mark of the invisible crown do not equal the World-Honored One’s. This is the contemplation of the true bodily form of Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva, called the tenth contemplation.]

When the bodhisattva lifts his foot, beneath his foot is the imprint of a thousand-spoked wheel, which naturally transforms into five hundred billion light platforms. When he sets his foot down, adamantine mani flowers scatter in all directions, leaving nothing uncovered. His remaining bodily marks are complete in all their secondary marks, no different from a Buddha’s. Only the fleshy mound upon his crown and the mark of the invisible crown do not equal the World-Honored One’s. The above is called the contemplation of the true bodily form of Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva, named the tenth contemplation.

[The mark of the thousand-spoked wheel] Beneath the feet is the imprint of a thousand-spoked wheel. This is the mark that designates one who governs all dharmas as a king. ‘Spoke’ means the spokes of a chariot wheel. [The mark of the invisible crown] This is the sixty-sixth of the Buddha’s eighty marks. Upon the Buddha’s crown a mound of flesh rises in the shape of a topknot, and within this mark no human or god can see its summit, hence it is called the mark of the invisible crown.

[The Buddha said to Ānanda: If one wishes to contemplate Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva, one should make this contemplation. One who makes this contemplation meets with no disasters, purifies and removes karmic obstacles, and erases the offenses of birth and death of countless kalpas. As for this bodhisattva, merely hearing his name brings immeasurable blessings — how much more so clear contemplation!]

The Buddha told Ānanda: If one wishes to contemplate Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva, one should make this contemplation. One who makes this contemplation meets with no disasters, purifies and removes karmic obstacles, and erases the offenses of birth and death of countless kalpas. As for Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva, merely hearing his name brings immeasurable blessings — how much more so clear contemplation!

[If there are those who wish to contemplate Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva, they should first contemplate the fleshy mound upon his crown, then contemplate the heavenly crown, and then contemplate the remaining marks in order, making them all clear and distinct, as if looking at something in the palm of the hand. One who makes this contemplation is called right contemplation; if one contemplates something else, it is called wrong contemplation.]

If there are those who wish to contemplate Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva, they should first contemplate the fleshy mound upon his crown, next the heavenly crown, and then the remaining marks in order, all of them clear and distinct, as if looking at something in the palm of the hand. One who makes this contemplation is called right contemplation; if one contemplates other things, it is called wrong contemplation.

blocks.text: Eleven. The Contemplation of Mahasthamaprapta

inline.s: [Next, contemplate Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva. The size of this bodhisattva’s body is also like Avalokitesvara’s. Each face of his halo is two hundred and twenty-five yojanas across, illumining two hundred and fifty yojanas. The light of his entire body illumines the lands of the ten directions, appearing as purple-gold, and all beings with the karmic connection see it.]

Next, contemplate Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva. The size of this bodhisattva’s body is also like Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva’s. Each face of his halo is two hundred and twenty-five yojanas across, illumining two hundred and fifty yojanas. The light of his entire body illumines the lands of the ten directions, appearing as purple-gold, and all beings with the karmic connection see it.

[Simply seeing the light of one pore of this bodhisattva, one sees the pure and wonderful light of the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions; therefore this bodhisattva is named Boundless Light. With the light of wisdom he illumines all things everywhere, causing beings to leave the three evil paths and attain unsurpassed power; therefore this bodhisattva is named Mahasthamaprapta.]

Simply seeing the light of one pore of this bodhisattva, one sees the pure and wonderful light of the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions; therefore this bodhisattva is named Boundless Light. With the light of wisdom he illumines all sentient beings everywhere, causing them to leave the three evil paths and attain unsurpassed power. Because this bodhisattva possesses the supreme and utmost great power, he is named Mahasthamaprapta (Great Strength Arrived).

[The three paths of suffering] Also called the three paths. That is, the path of fire, the path of knives, and the path of blood, which are the same as the three evil paths of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals — the places into which beings are drawn by the various evil karmas of body, speech, and mind. 1. The path of fire, that is, the hell path: because the beings there are constantly tormented by the heat of boiling cauldrons and blazing furnaces, and because fires gather there in great number, it is called the path of fire. 2. The path of knives, that is, the hungry ghost path: because the beings there constantly suffer from being driven and pressed by knives and staves, it is called the path of knives. 3. The path of blood, that is, the animal path: because the beings there, the strong subduing the weak, devour one another, drinking blood and eating flesh, it is called the path of blood. The word ‘path’ (tu) here is the simplified form of another character tu, and is the same as the character for ‘way’.

[This bodhisattva’s heavenly crown has five hundred jewelled lotus flowers, and each and every jewelled flower has five hundred jewelled daises. Within each and every dais, the marks of the breadth and length of the pure and wonderful lands of the Buddhas of the ten directions all appear.]

This bodhisattva’s heavenly crown has five hundred jewelled lotus flowers, and each and every jewelled flower has five hundred jewelled daises. Within each and every dais, the marks of the vast breadth and length of the pure and wonderful lands of the Buddhas of the ten directions all appear.

[The fleshy mound upon his crown is like a padma flower. Upon the fleshy mound there is a jewelled vase filled with all manner of light, in which the Buddha’s work appears everywhere. His remaining bodily marks are no different from Avalokitesvara’s. When this bodhisattva walks, all the worlds of the ten directions quake. Wherever the ground quakes, five hundred billion jewelled flowers appear, each and every jewelled flower adorned and towering on high, like the Land of Ultimate Bliss.]

The fleshy mound upon his crown is like a red lotus flower. Upon the fleshy mound there is a jewelled vase filled with all manner of light, in which the Buddha’s work appears everywhere. His remaining bodily marks are entirely the same as Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva’s. When this bodhisattva walks, the earth of all the worlds of the ten directions quakes. Wherever the ground quakes, five hundred billion jewelled flowers appear, each and every jewelled flower adorned and towering on high, like the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
[Padma flower] Rendered in meaning as: the red lotus flower, the red lotus.

[When this bodhisattva sits, the land of the seven treasures quakes at once. From the Golden Light Buddha land below to the Light King Buddha land above, in the space between them, immeasurable dust-mote numbers of emanated Buddhas of Immeasurable Life, emanated Avalokitesvaras, and emanated Mahasthamapraptas all gather like clouds in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, filling the air, seated upon lotus thrones, proclaiming the wonderful Dharma and saving suffering beings.]

When this bodhisattva sits, the land of the seven treasures quakes at once. From the Golden Light Buddha land below to the Light King Buddha land above, in the space between them, immeasurable dust-mote numbers of emanated Buddhas of Immeasurable Life, emanated Avalokitesvara Bodhisattvas, and emanated Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattvas all gather like clouds in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, filling the air, seated upon lotus thrones, proclaiming the wonderful Dharma and saving suffering beings.
[Dust-mote number] Also called the number of fine dust motes; a simile for a number that is exceedingly great.

[One who makes this contemplation is said to see Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva; this is the contemplation of Mahasthamaprapta’s bodily form. One who contemplates this bodhisattva is said to make the eleventh contemplation, erasing the offenses of birth and death of countless asamkhyeya kalpas. One who makes this contemplation does not dwell in a womb and constantly roams the pure and wonderful lands of the Buddhas. When this contemplation is accomplished, one is said to have fully contemplated Avalokitesvara and Mahasthamaprapta.]

One who contemplates thus is said to see Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva, and is said to contemplate Mahasthamaprapta’s bodily form. One who contemplates this bodhisattva is said to make the eleventh contemplation, erasing the offenses of birth and death of countless asamkhyeya kalpas. One who makes this contemplation does not dwell in a womb and constantly roams the pure and wonderful lands of the Buddhas. When this contemplation is accomplished, one is said to have fully contemplated Avalokitesvara and Mahasthamaprapta.

[Not dwelling in a womb] Not undergoing the suffering of transmigration through entering a womb and being born from one. [Asamkhyeya] Rendered in Chinese as ‘incalculable’. Reckoned by the scale in which ten thousand times ten thousand makes one hundred million and ten thousand hundred millions makes one trillion, one asamkhyeya is a number of trillions multiplied by ten thousand seven times over.

blocks.text: Twelve. The Contemplation of the Universal Vision

inline.s: [When one sees this matter, one should rouse the thought that one’s own mind is born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, sitting cross-legged within a lotus flower, forming the thought of the lotus closing and the thought of the lotus opening. When the lotus opens, five hundred hues of light come to illumine the body. Form the thought of the eyes opening, and see the Buddha and the bodhisattvas filling the sky. The sounds issued by the water, the birds, and the trees, and by all the Buddhas, all proclaim the wonderful Dharma, in accord with the twelve divisions of the scriptures. If one rises from samādhi, one remembers and holds them without losing them.]

When the contemplation of Mahasthamaprapta is accomplished, one should contemplate in this way: that oneself is born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, sitting cross-legged within a lotus flower, forming the thought of the lotus closing and the thought of the lotus opening. When the lotus opens, five hundred kinds of colored light come to illumine the body. Form the thought of the eyes opening, and see the Buddha and the bodhisattvas filling the sky. The sounds issued by the water, the birds, and the trees, and by all the Buddhas, all proclaim the wonderful Dharma, in accord with the twelve divisions of the scriptures. If one rises from samādhi, one should likewise remember and hold them without losing them.

[The twelve divisions of the scriptures] The content of all the scriptures may be divided into twelve categories, called the twelve divisions of the scriptures, also called the twelve-part teaching. 1. Long lines (prose), setting forth the marks of the Dharma directly in prose, without restriction as to sentence or phrase; because the lines are long, they are called long lines. 2. Repeated verses, which, having been proclaimed before, are concluded afterwards with verses, with the meaning of proclaiming them again, hence ‘repeated verses’. 3. Independent verses, verses not based upon the meaning of the prose that precedes them but raised independently. 4. Causes and conditions, recounting the causes and conditions of seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, or of the Buddha’s preaching and teaching. 5. Past lives of disciples, scriptures recording the Buddha’s account of the past-life causes and conditions of his various disciples. 6. Past lives of the Buddha, scriptures recording the Buddha’s account of his own past-life causes and conditions. 7. Marvels never before spoken, scriptures recording the Buddha’s manifestation of all manner of miraculous and inconceivable powers. 8. Parables, scriptures in which the Buddha speaks various parables to make it easy for sentient beings to awaken. 9. Discussions, scriptures consisting of questions and answers on the principles of the Dharma. 10. Unrequested teachings, such as the Amitābha Sutra, spoken by the Buddha without anyone having asked. 11. Vaipulya (vast and expansive), scriptures in which the Buddha sets forth the true principle, upright and vast. 12. Prophecies, or predictions: the record of the Buddha’s prediction to bodhisattvas or hearers of the name and time of their attaining Buddhahood.

Having seen this, it is called seeing Amitayus, the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, and the Land of Ultimate Bliss. This is the universal contemplation, known as the twelfth contemplation. The Buddha of Immeasurable Life has countless transformation bodies, and together with Avalokitesvara and Mahasthamaprapta, he constantly comes to the place where this practicer dwells.

Thus, when this contemplation is perfected, it is called seeing the Buddha of Immeasurable Life and the Land of Ultimate Bliss. It is called the universal contemplation, known as the twelfth contemplation. The Buddha of Immeasurable Life has countless transformation bodies, and together with Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva and Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva, he constantly comes to the place where this practicer dwells.

blocks.text: 13. The Contemplation of Miscellaneous Forms

inline.s: The Buddha told Ānanda and Queen Vaidehī: If one wishes to be reborn in the West with a sincere mind, one should first contemplate an image sixteen feet in height, standing upon the water of the pond. As said earlier, the body of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life is boundless, beyond the reach of the mind of ordinary beings; yet because of the power of the Tathagata's past vows, whoever recollects and contemplates him will surely succeed.

The Buddha told Ānanda and Queen Vaidehī: If one wishes to be reborn in the West with a sincere mind, one should first contemplate the image of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, sixteen feet in height, standing upon the water of the pond. As said earlier, the body of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life is boundless, not within the reach of the mind of ordinary beings; yet because of the power of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life's past vows, whoever recollects and contemplates him will surely succeed.

But merely contemplating an image of the Buddha already yields immeasurable merit, how much more so contemplating the Buddha's complete body of marks! Amitābha Buddha, through his transcendent powers, transforms freely throughout the ten directions. Sometimes he manifests a great body filling the entire sky; sometimes a small body, sixteen feet or eight feet. Whatever form he manifests, it is all of true gold color, with its halo of light, its transformation Buddhas, and its jewelled lotus flowers, as described above.

Merely contemplating an image of the Buddha already yields immeasurable merit, how much more so contemplating the Buddha's complete body of marks! Amitābha Buddha, through his transcendent powers, transforms freely throughout the ten directions. Sometimes he manifests a great body filling the entire sky; sometimes a small body, sixteen feet or eight feet. Whatever form he manifests, it is all of true gold color, with its halo of light, its transformation Buddhas, and its jewelled lotus flowers, as described above.
As for the halo of light and the transformation Buddhas, these are as the earlier scripture passage said:

The halo of light of that Buddha is like a hundred billion great trichiliocosms. Within that halo of light there are a hundred million billion nayuta transformation Buddhas, as numerous as the sand of the Ganges. Each transformation Buddha likewise has many countless transformation bodhisattvas as his attendants.

Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva and Mahasthamaprapta, in all places, have bodies the same as sentient beings. But by observing only the distinguishing marks of their heads, one knows this is Avalokitesvara, and knows this is Mahasthamaprapta. These two bodhisattvas assist Amitābha Buddha in universally transforming all beings. This is the contemplation of miscellaneous forms, known as the thirteenth contemplation.

Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva and Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva, in all places, have bodies the same as sentient beings. But by observing only the distinguishing marks of the heads of these bodhisattvas, one knows this is Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva, and knows this is Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva. These two bodhisattvas assist Amitābha Buddha in universally transforming all sentient beings. The above contemplation is called the contemplation of miscellaneous forms, known as the thirteenth contemplation.

As for 'but observing only the distinguishing marks of the heads, one knows this is Avalokitesvara and knows this is Mahasthamaprapta': the crown of Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva has a standing Buddha (as the earlier scripture passage says:
Within his heavenly crown is a standing transformation Buddha.
), and the topknot of Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva has a jewelled flask (as the earlier scripture passage says:
Upon his flesh topknot is a jewelled flask, holding every kind of light, universally displaying the Buddha's works.
). By these one can distinguish whether it is Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva, and whether it is Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva.

blocks.text: 14. The Contemplation of the Highest Grade of Rebirth (the assembly of bodhisattvas)

inline.s: The following three contemplations — the highest grade of rebirth, the middle grade, and the lowest grade — contemplate the manner of rebirth of beings already reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss (the assembly of bodhisattvas, the assembly of sravakas, and the assembly of the common folk). Because this scripture contemplates the dependent and primary retributions of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, and not the beings of the Sahā world. In the passage above the Buddha said:
The Tathagata now teaches Queen Vaidehī and all sentient beings of future ages to contemplate the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Within the nine grades: the three stages of the highest grade are the assembly of bodhisattvas of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss; the three stages of the middle grade are the assembly of sravakas of that land; the three stages of the lowest grade are the assembly of the common folk of that land. The three classes and nine grades gather together all the holy and ordinary beings of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Dependent and primary retributions: the dependent retribution and the primary retribution. The land, buildings, dwellings, and implements, being what the body depends upon, are called the dependent retribution; the body of sentient beings, which is a provisional union of the five aggregates, is the result of karmic actions created in the past and is called the primary retribution. The five aggregates: the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness. These five are called aggregates because they are produced through accumulation; and because they can cover over a person's true nature, causing delusion and inversion and the creation of all kinds of karma, they are also called the five coverings. Among them, the aggregate of form refers to matter and is called form dharmas; the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness belong to the mind and are called mind dharmas. These are the five great elements that constitute body and mind. Of these, the aggregate of form is the physical body, and the other four aggregates — feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness — are the mind.
The Buddha told Ānanda and Queen Vaidehī: All beings who are reborn in the West are of nine grades:
The Buddha told Ānanda and Queen Vaidehī: Those who have already been reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss are altogether of nine grades.

blocks.text: (1) The Highest Stage of the Highest Grade

inline.s: As for those of the highest stage of the highest grade: if any sentient being wishes to be reborn in that land, he should develop three kinds of minds, and he will thereupon be reborn. What are these three? First, the mind of utmost sincerity; second, the deep mind; third, the mind of dedication of merit and the making of vows. Whoever is endowed with these three minds will surely be reborn in that land.

As for those of the highest stage of the highest grade: if any sentient being wishes to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, he should develop three kinds of minds, and he will thereupon be reborn. Which three? First, the mind of utmost sincerity; second, the deep mind; third, the mind of dedication of merit and the making of vows. Whoever is endowed with these three minds will surely be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

The mind of utmost sincerity: 'utmost' means leaving no room for anything else; 'sincerity' means this single mind alone. Being resolved to seek rebirth in the Pure Land, cultivating with undivided attention without interruption — this is called utmost sincerity. The deep mind: this is the mind of deep faith. With a deep mind one believes and understands and is always self-possessed and pure.

Dedication of merit: 'turning one's own roots of goodness toward a goal' — concentrating the power of the roots of goodness one has created upon a certain objective, so that it may be realized as swiftly as possible. For example, all the various good deeds cultivated through one's three kinds of action (bodily, verbal, and mental action), and even all the merits of confession, entreaty, and so on, are dedicated to all sentient beings of the Dharma realm, that they may together realize bodhi. The Commentary on the Treatise on Rebirth says:
Dedication means turning one's own merit and offering it universally to sentient beings, that together they may see Amitābha Tathagata and be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
The verse 'Making Vows of Refuge in the Three Jewels' by Master Shandao says:
May this merit be given universally to all equally; may we together awaken the bodhi mind and be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
(from the Four-Volume Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra)

Making vows: to establish a firm vow, resolved to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. The mind of dedication and of making vows: the mind that both dedicates merit and makes vows — all roots of goodness, wholly from a mind of genuine deep faith, are dedicated to all sentient beings of the Dharma realm, and one vows to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Roots of goodness: the goodness of the three actions of body, speech, and mind, which being firmly planted cannot be uprooted — this is called root. Moreover, goodness can produce marvelous fruits and give rise to further goodness, and so it is called root.
The Lingzhi Commentary (the Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, Song
dynasty, composed by the monk Yuanzhao of Lingzhi Chongfu Monastery on West Lake) says:
'If
(these three minds)
are matched to the three gatherings
(the three-gathering pure precepts)
: the first is the observance of the rules of discipline
(the precept of observing the rules of discipline)
, cutting off all evil without exception, and so it must be utmost sincerity. The second is the gathering of wholesome dharmas
(the precept of gathering wholesome dharmas)
, cultivating every good without omission, and so it must grow ever deep. The third is the gathering of sentient beings
(the precept of gathering sentient beings)

, delivering all beings without exception, and so it must be the dedication of merit. If matched to the three Buddhas: the first is the virtue of the cessation of defilement, which is the dharmakāya Buddha; the second is the virtue of wisdom, which is the sambhogakaya Buddha; the third is the virtue of grace, which is the nirmanakaya Buddha. Since the fruit is three Buddhas, the cause must be three minds; not one may be lacking.'

The three-gathering pure precepts: the precept of observing the rules of discipline, the precept of gathering wholesome dharmas, and the precept of gathering sentient beings. The precept of observing the rules of discipline is to observe the Buddha's teachings and do no evil; the precept of gathering wholesome dharmas is to practice all good; the precept of gathering sentient beings is to cultivate all wholesome dharmas broadly so as to benefit sentient beings. The first two are self-benefit, and the third is benefiting others. Combining these two benefits for self and others is called the perfect fulfillment of the two benefits, and it is what all Mahayana scholars should uphold. The virtues of cessation, wisdom, and grace: the Buddha's three virtues of benefiting himself and others. First, the virtue of cessation — the Buddha has cut off all afflictions, is pure and unconditioned, and is free and at ease. Second, the virtue of wisdom — the Buddha's wisdom is deep and vast, knowing all things, and he is called one who knows all. Third, the virtue of grace — the Buddha's compassion is vast, and he vows to deliver all sentient beings without partiality or favoritism; among the beings of the three realms and six paths, none who has the connection fails to be delivered. Among these three virtues, wisdom and cessation belong to self-benefit, while grace belongs to benefiting others.

There are again three kinds of sentient beings who will be reborn there. What are these three? First, those with a compassionate mind who do not kill and who observe all the precepts; second, those who recite and read the Mahayana Vaipulya scriptures; third, those who cultivate the six recollections, dedicate their merit and make vows, wishing to be reborn in that Buddha land. Endowed with these merits, whether for one day or even seven days, they will be reborn there.
There are also beings who accomplish three kinds of practice (
xing

) of karmic merit who will be reborn there. Which three kinds of practice? First, a compassionate mind that does not kill, observing all the precepts; second, reciting and reading the Mahayana scriptures; third, cultivating the six recollections, dedicating merit and making vows, wishing to be reborn in that Buddha land. Whether for one day or even seven days, those who accomplish (are endowed with) the merit of these three kinds of practice will thereupon be reborn.

The three kinds of sentient beings: sentient beings who cultivate all three kinds of practice together. The Outline Commentary (the Outline Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, Qing
dynasty, by Peng Jiqing) says:

'By the three kinds of sentient beings is meant beings who cultivate the three kinds of practice together, not those who each cultivate only one. For faith and vow support each other, and understanding and practice advance each other. If even one is deficient, one cannot enter the Way.'

Practice and karmic action: the actions created by body, speech, and mind. The Devadatta chapter of the Lotus Sutra says, and the Scripture of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, spoken by the Buddha, says:
The karmic retribution of practice and action is inconceivable.
Observing all the precepts: the precepts here refer to the bodhisattva precepts. Master Shandao says:

'By observing all the precepts: if it refers to the capacities of humans, gods, and the two vehicles, it is called the lesser precepts; if it refers to persons of great mind and great practice, it is called the bodhisattva precepts. If this precept is reckoned by stage, then for those of the three stages of the upper grade it is called the bodhisattva precept.'
(from the Four-Volume Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra)

The Mahayana Vaipulya scriptures: these are the Mahayana scriptures; 'Vaipulya' scripture is a general term for the Mahayana sutras. The six recollections: first, recollection of the Buddha — recollect that the Buddha is endowed with the ten epithets, has great compassion, great pity, and great light, has measureless transcendent powers, and can pull beings out of suffering; I wish to be like the Buddha. Second, recollection of the Dharma — recollect that all the teachings spoken by the Tathagata have great merit and are the supreme wondrous medicine; I wish to realize them and give them to sentient beings. Third, recollection of the Sangha — recollect that the Sangha are disciples of the Tathagata, have attained the undefiled Dharma, are fully endowed with precepts, meditation, and wisdom, and are the field of merit for the world; I too wish to cultivate the practice of the Sangha. Fourth, recollection of the precepts — recollect that observance of the precepts has great power and can guard against all evil; I wish to uphold the precepts with vigor. Fifth, recollection of giving — recollect that giving has great merit, that it can both relieve others' suffering and remove one's own stinginess and greed; I wish to benefit all sentient beings universally through giving. Sixth, recollection of the heavens — recollect that the heavens have natural happiness, all owing to the cause of diligently cultivating the ten wholesome actions in the past; I too wish to cultivate wholesome karma diligently, so that wholesome causes may bring wholesome fruits.
Being endowed with these merits for one day or even seven days: for one day or even seven days, accomplishing the merit of these three kinds of practice

one day or even seven days) — one day or even seven days is an illustrative expression, an abbreviated way of speaking. To state it in detail, for example as the World-Honored One said in the Great Mindfulness Foundation Sutra:
'Monks! Anyone who, in this manner, correctly cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness for seven years may expect one of two fruits: in this very life attaining supreme wisdom
(realizing the fruit of arhatship)
, or, if the five aggregates remain, attaining the fruit of non-returning
(realizing the fruit of anagami)
. Monks! Not to speak of seven years,
Monks! Not to speak of six years,
Monks! Not to speak of one year,
Monks! Not to speak of seven months,
Monks! Not to speak of one month,

Monks! Not to speak of half a month; if anyone, in this manner, correctly cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness for seven days, he may expect one of two fruits: in this very life attaining supreme wisdom, or, if the five aggregates remain, attaining the fruit of non-returning.'

The four fruits: in cultivating the four noble truths there are four fruits: the fruit of stream-enterer, the fruit of once-returner, the fruit of non-returner, and the fruit of arhat. Among them, the fourth fruit, the arhat, is the highest; one who attains this fruit is released from birth and death and no longer undergoes a future existence.

When he is reborn in that land, because this person is vigorous and courageous, Amitābha Tathagata, together with Avalokitesvara, Mahasthamaprapta, countless transformation Buddhas, hundreds and thousands of monks, the great assembly of sravakas, measureless gods, and palaces of the seven treasures — with Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva holding the adamant throne and Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva — come before the practicer.

When he is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, because this person is vigorous and courageous, Amitābha Buddha, together with Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva, Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva, countless transformation Buddhas, hundreds and thousands of monks, the great assembly of sravakas, measureless gods, and palaces of the seven treasures — with Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva holding the adamant throne and Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva — come before the practicer.

Amitābha Buddha emits a great light of illumination, shining upon the practicer's body, and together with the various bodhisattvas extends his hand to welcome him. Avalokitesvara, Mahasthamaprapta, and countless bodhisattvas praise the practicer and encourage his mind.

Amitābha Buddha emits a great light of illumination, shining upon the practicer's body, and together with the various bodhisattvas extends his hand to welcome him. Avalokitesvara, Mahasthamaprapta, and countless bodhisattvas praise the practicer and encourage his mind.

When the practicer sees this, he rejoices and leaps with joy. He sees his own body riding the adamant throne, following behind the Buddha, and in the twinkling of an eye he is reborn in that land. Once reborn there, he sees the Buddha's physical body endowed with all the marks, and sees the various bodhisattvas endowed with all their marks; the light and the jeweled grove proclaim the wondrous Dharma. Upon hearing it, he immediately realizes the patient endurance of the unproduced, and in a moment he passes before the Buddhas throughout the ten directions, and before each Buddha in turn receives the prophecy of his future Buddhahood. Returning to that land, he attains measureless, hundreds and thousands of gates of dharani. This is called one of the highest stage of the highest grade.

When the practicer sees this, he rejoices and leaps with joy. He sees his own body riding the adamant throne, following behind Amitābha Buddha, and in the twinkling of an eye he is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Once reborn there, he sees the Buddha's physical body endowed with all the marks, and sees the various bodhisattvas endowed with all their marks; the light and the jeweled grove proclaim the wondrous Dharma. Upon hearing this wondrous Dharma, he immediately realizes the patient endurance of the unproduced, and in a moment he passes before the Buddhas throughout the ten directions, and before each Buddha in turn receives the prophecy. Returning to that land, he attains measureless, hundreds and thousands of gates of dharani. This is called one of the highest stage of the highest grade.
The adamant throne: a throne made of adamant. A moment (
yu

): an instant; a moment. The prophecy: receiving from the Buddha the prediction that one will in the future certainly become a Buddha. The gates of dharani: dharani, in Chinese translation, means 'to hold and maintain.' Through the method of holding and maintaining, the bodhisattva accommodates the speech and sounds of all sentient beings, guides them in right faith, causes them to extinguish all evil thoughts, and to practice all wholesome dharmas — this is called the bodhisattva's gates of dharani.

blocks.text: (2) The Middle Stage of the Highest Grade

inline.s: As for those of the middle stage of the highest grade: they need not uphold and recite the Vaipulya scriptures; but they well understand the meaning and drift, are not disturbed in mind regarding the first principle, deeply believe in cause and effect, and do not slander the Mahayana. With this merit they dedicate it, and vow to seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

As for those of the middle stage of the highest grade: they need not uphold and recite the Mahayana scriptures; but they well understand the meaning and drift of the Buddha's teaching, are not disturbed in mind regarding the first principle, deeply believe in cause and effect, and do not slander the Mahayana. With this merit they dedicate it, and vow to seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Not needing to uphold and recite the Vaipulya scriptures: The Wondrous Axiom Commentary (the Wondrous Axiom Commentary on the Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, Song
dynasty, a commentary-rendering by the monk Zhili of Siming) says:
'By not needing, it refers to a person who holds to the meaning
(a person who delights in deeply investigating the meaning)
, and does not delight in recitation. He takes but one line or one verse from the scripture and deeply exhausts its purport. Regarding the deep and vast principle that transcends speech and thought
(concerning the deep and vast principle that transcends speech and thought)

, his mind is not disturbed. Moreover, his mind abides in the middle way and is not disturbed by either of the two extremes. He clearly understands that cause and effect are all true reality, and this is called deep faith. Though he has not studied exhaustively, if he hears the great teaching or its differing explanations given in accord with capacities, he knows that they reveal a single principle, and he gives rise to no doubt or slander.'

The middle way: nowhere leaning toward emptiness, nowhere leaning toward existence; neither empty nor existent, yet both empty and existent; not falling into either of the two extremes; perfectly interfused and unobstructed — this is called the middle way.
The first principle: the supreme, perfect, and ultimate truth. The true reality of all dharmas is the first principle. The Buddha said:

All dharmas are wholly false and illusory; wherever they cease, that is called true, that is called true reality, that is called the Dharma realm, that is called ultimate wisdom, that is called the truth of the first principle, that is called the emptiness of the first principle.
The first principle is also called the truth of the first principle. 'Truth' means the principle that is true and without error.
(from the Great Parinirvāṇa Sutra
, chapter forty.) The true reality of all dharmas: this is the actual condition of all dharmas. The Buddha Repository Sutra says:
What is called the true reality of all dharmas? It is that all dharmas are ultimately empty, entirely without existence.
The Great Parinirvāṇa Sutra says:
All dharmas are like illusory appearances; the Tathagata, within them, through the power of skill-in-means, is not attached to anything.
The Lotus Sutra says:
The bodhisattva-mahasattva contemplates all dharmas as empty, as true reality, without inversion, without agitation, without regression, without turning.
For a detailed discussion of the true reality of all dharmas, see
The True Reality of All Dharmas
article.

When a person who practices this is about to end his life, Amitābha Buddha, together with Avalokitesvara, Mahasthamaprapta, and surrounded by the measureless great assembly and retinue, comes bearing a purple-golden throne to the practicer and praises him, saying: 'Dharma-son, you practice the Mahayana and understand the first principle; therefore I now come to welcome you.' Together with a thousand transformation Buddhas, they extend their hands at the same moment.

When one who practices this is about to end his life, Amitābha Buddha, together with Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva and Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva and surrounded by the measureless great assembly and retinue, comes bearing a purple-golden throne to the practicer and praises him, saying: 'Dharma-son, you practice the Mahayana and understand the first principle; therefore I now come to welcome you.' Together with a thousand transformation Buddhas, they extend their hands to welcome him at the same moment.
Dharma-son: one who follows the Buddha's Way and is nourished by the Dharma.

The practicer sees himself seated on the purple-golden throne, with palms together and hands clasped, praising the Buddhas. In the space of a single thought he is born in the pond of the seven treasures of that land. This purple-golden throne is like a great jeweled flower that opens after a single night. The practicer's body becomes the color of pure gold, and beneath his feet there are likewise lotus flowers of the seven treasures. The Buddha and the bodhisattvas all emit light, shining upon the practicer's body, and his eyes immediately open and grow clear.

The practicer sees himself seated on the purple-golden throne, with palms together and hands clasped, praising the Buddhas. In the space of a single thought he is born in the pond of the seven treasures of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. This purple-golden throne is like a great jeweled flower that opens after a single night. The practicer's body becomes the color of pure gold, and beneath his feet there are likewise lotus flowers of the seven treasures. The Buddha and the bodhisattvas all emit light, shining upon the practicer's body, and his eyes immediately open and grow clear, so that he sees the Buddha distinctly.

Clasping the hands: a method of reverent salutation in India, also called the adamant palms together. It is bringing the palms together and crossing the fingers of both hands. The eyes immediately open and grow clear: the eyes immediately open and grow clear, and one sees the Buddha distinctly. Later, in the passage on the lowest stage of the highest grade, it says that one must pass twenty-one days before seeing the Buddha distinctly. The scripture says:

After one day and one night the lotus opens, and within seven days one comes to see the Buddha. Though one sees the Buddha's body, one's mind is not yet clear regarding the many excellent marks; only after twenty-one days does one see him distinctly.

Because of the habits formed in past lives, he universally hears all the voices, purely proclaiming the deep first principle. He then descends from the golden throne, bows to the Buddha, clasps his palms together, and praises the World-Honored One. After seven days he immediately attains non-retrogression with respect to anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. He is at once able to fly to the ten directions, passing before the Buddhas and cultivating all the samādhis at the abodes of the Buddhas. After one small kalpa he attains the patient endurance of the unproduced and receives the prophecy in person. This is called one of the middle stage of the highest grade.

Because of the habits formed in past lives, he universally hears all the sounds, all proclaiming the deep first principle. He then descends from the purple-golden throne, bows to the Buddha, clasps his palms together, and praises the World-Honored One. After seven days he immediately attains non-retrogression with respect to Buddha wisdom (anuttara-samyak-sambodhi). He is at once able to fly to the ten directions, making offerings to the Buddhas and cultivating all kinds of samādhi at the abodes of the Buddhas. After one small kalpa he attains the patient endurance of the unproduced and, before each Buddha in turn, receives the prophecy. This is called one of the middle stage of the highest grade. One small kalpa: the human lifespan, beginning at eighty-four thousand years, decreases by one year every hundred years until it reaches ten years; then, starting from ten years, it increases by one year every hundred years until it returns to the original eighty-four thousand years. One such decrease and increase constitutes a small kalpa. It is equal to sixteen million, seven hundred and ninety-eight thousand years.

Because of the habits formed in past lives: because of the habits of past lives in well understanding the meaning and drift, in being undisturbed in mind regarding the first principle, in deeply believing in cause and effect, and in not slandering the Mahayana. Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi: the name of Buddha wisdom, translated into Chinese as the supreme right and perfect enlightenment — that is, the supreme wisdom that truly and equally realizes all truth.

Those of the highest stage of the highest grade, upon being reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, see the Buddha immediately; but those of the middle stage of the highest grade must wait for the purple-golden throne, like a great jeweled flower, to open after a night before they see the Buddha. The former, in a moment, pass before the Buddhas; the latter require seven days. The former receive the prophecy from the Buddhas immediately; the latter require a small kalpa before attaining the patient endurance of the unproduced and the prophecy of the Buddhas.

blocks.text: (3) The Lowest Stage of the Highest Grade

inline.s: As for those of the lowest stage of the highest grade: they likewise believe in cause and effect, do not slander the Mahayana, and only awaken the mind of the supreme Way. With this merit they dedicate it, and vow to seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

As for those of the lowest stage of the highest grade: they likewise believe in cause and effect, do not slander the Mahayana, and only awaken the conviction and resolve to seek the supreme Way. Moreover, with this merit they dedicate it, and vow to seek rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

The mind of the supreme Way: the conviction and resolve to vow to seek the supreme Way. The supreme Way: the Way attained by the Tathagata, beyond which there is nothing higher, and so it is called the supreme Way. The Skillful Means chapter of the Lotus Sutra says:
Uprightly setting aside the skillful means, he solely proclaims the supreme Way.
The Lifespan chapter says:
He always thinks thus: by what means may I cause sentient beings to enter the supreme Way and quickly accomplish the Buddha body?
The chapter on Encouraging the Practice says:
I do not cherish my body and life; I only cherish the supreme Way.

For those of the middle stage of the highest grade, the distinguishing practice is to understand the truth of the first principle. For those of the lowest stage of the highest grade, the distinguishing practice is solely to awaken the mind of the supreme Way.

When that practicer is about to end his life, Amitābha Buddha, together with Avalokitesvara, Mahasthamaprapta, and the various retinue, bearing golden lotus flowers, transform into five hundred transformation Buddhas and come to welcome this person. The five hundred transformation Buddhas extend their hands at the same moment and praise him, saying: 'Dharma-son, you are now pure, and have awakened the mind of the supreme Way; I have come to welcome you.'

When this practicer is about to end his life, Amitābha Buddha, together with Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva, Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva, and the various retinue, bearing golden lotus flowers, transform into five hundred transformation Buddhas and come to welcome him. The five hundred transformation Buddhas extend their hands at the same moment and praise him, saying: 'Dharma-son, you are now pure, and have awakened the mind of the supreme Way; I have come to welcome you.'

When he sees this, he immediately sees his own body seated on a golden lotus flower; once seated, the flower closes, and he follows after the World-Honored One and is reborn in the pond of the seven treasures. After one day and one night the lotus opens, and within seven days he comes to see the Buddha. Though he sees the Buddha's body, his mind is not clear regarding the many excellent marks; only after twenty-one days does he see him distinctly.

When this practicer sees this (the Buddhas and bodhisattvas coming to welcome him), he immediately sees his own body seated on a golden lotus flower; once seated, the golden lotus closes, and he follows after the World-Honored One and is reborn in the pond of the seven treasures of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Only after one day and one night does the golden lotus open, and within seven days he comes to see the Buddha. Though he sees the Buddha's body, his mind is not clear regarding the various excellent marks of the Buddha; only after twenty-one days does he see him distinctly.

He hears the sounds of the assembly, all proclaiming the wondrous Dharma. He travels throughout the ten directions, making offerings to all the Buddhas, and before the Buddhas he hears the deep Dharma. After three small kalpas he attains the understanding gate of the hundred dharmas and abides in the ground of joy. This is called one of the lowest stage of the highest grade.

He universally hears all the sounds, all proclaiming the wondrous Dharma of the supreme Way. Thus he travels throughout the ten directions, making offerings to all the Buddhas, and before the Buddhas he hears the deep Dharma. After three small kalpas he attains the understanding gate of the hundred dharmas and abides in the ground of joy. This is called one of the lowest stage of the highest grade.

The understanding gate of the hundred dharmas: the gate of wisdom that a bodhisattva attains in the first ground (the ground of joy), through which he can penetrate the true nature of the hundred dharmas. The hundred dharmas: also called the hundred dharmas of the five categories; they comprehensively encompass all things in the universe. The five categories: mind dharmas, mental-factors dharmas, form dharmas, dharmas not corresponding with mind, and unconditioned dharmas. The hundred dharmas: mind dharmas number eight and are the self-nature of consciousness; mental-factors dharmas number fifty-one and belong to consciousness; form dharmas number eleven and are transformations of the mind dharmas and mental-factors dharmas; dharmas not corresponding with mind number twenty-four and are the categories of the mind dharmas, mental-factors dharmas, and form dharmas, being also dharmas that correspond neither with mind nor with form; unconditioned dharmas number six. Altogether they form a hundred dharmas.

The ten grounds: among the fifty-two stages of the bodhisattva's practice, the fifth group of ten stages is called the ten grounds. Through these ten grounds one gradually opens the Buddha realm and accomplishes the wisdom of all species; being already on the stage of sages, it is also called the ten sages. First, the ground of joy: when the bodhisattva has fulfilled the practice of the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa, first glimpses the mind-nature, breaks through the delusion of views, and realizes the emptiness of the two (self and dharmas), accomplishes the perfection of giving, and gives rise to great joy — hence it is called the ground of joy.
