Second, the ground of freedom from defilement: the bodhisattva cuts off the delusion of thought, removes the offense of transgression, makes his body pure, accomplishes the perfection of precepts, and is free from all defilement — hence it is called the ground of freedom from defilement. Third, the ground of radiating light: the bodhisattva extinguishes the darkness of ignorance and attains the three insights, accomplishes the perfection of patience, and the light of his mind shines forth — hence it is called the ground of radiating light. Fourth, the ground of flaming wisdom: the bodhisattva is completely endowed with the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, further cultivates the powers, the fearlessnesses, and the dharmas not shared with others, and, far from idleness, accomplishes the perfection of vigor, so that the flame of his wisdom burns brightly — hence it is called the ground of flaming wisdom. Fifth, the ground of supreme difficult conquest: for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, the bodhisattva studies the various arts externally while within he accomplishes the perfection of meditation; it is supremely difficult to overcome — hence it is called the ground of supreme difficult conquest. Sixth, the ground of presence: the bodhisattva dwells in the method of liberation, cultivates the samādhi of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, accomplishes the perfection of wisdom, and causes all differing appearances present before him to be utterly dissolved — hence it is called the ground of presence. Seventh, the ground of far going: the bodhisattva cuts off the fine manifestations of the fruits of karma, rises to supreme practice, broadly transforms sentient beings, accomplishes the perfection of skill-in-means, and prepares the provisions for the far journey — hence it is called the ground of far going. Eighth, the ground of immovability: the bodhisattva dwells in the patient endurance of the unproduced, cuts off all his previous activities, his body and mind are as still as empty space, and he accomplishes the perfection of vows; with a mind akin to nirvāṇa, he is serene and unmoving — hence it is called the ground of immovability. Ninth, the ground of good wisdom: the bodhisattva extinguishes the marks of mind, realizes the freedom of wisdom, is fully endowed with the ten powers, and clearly knows all places and non-places; he accomplishes the perfection of power and skillfully applies understanding — hence it is called the ground of good wisdom. Tenth, the ground of the Dharma cloud: the bodhisattva broadly gathers measureless Dharma, increases boundless merit and wisdom, knows completely the mind-action of all sentient beings, and according to their superior, middling, and inferior faculties, teaches them the three vehicles; he accomplishes the perfection of wisdom, and like a great cloud, rains the great Dharma rain — hence it is called the ground of the Dharma cloud. The fifty-two stages: from an ordinary being to Buddhahood, the bodhisattva passes altogether through fifty-two stages, namely: the ten faiths, the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten dedications of merit, the ten grounds, equal enlightenment, and wondrous enlightenment.

With regard to seeing the Buddha when the flower opens: those of the highest stage of the highest grade see him at once when the time comes; those of the middle stage of the highest grade see him only after a night; those of the lowest stage of the highest grade see him only within seven days, and only after twenty-one days can they see him clearly.
This is called the contemplation of rebirth in the upper class, known as the fourteenth contemplation.

The contemplation of the above three aspects of rebirth (the aspect of the highest stage of the highest grade, the middle stage, and the lowest stage) is together called the contemplation of rebirth in the upper class, known as the fourteenth contemplation.

blocks.text: 15. The Contemplation of the Middle Grade of Rebirth (the assembly of sravakas)
(1) The Highest Stage of the Middle Grade

inline.s: The Buddha told Ānanda and Queen Vaidehī: As for those of the highest stage of the middle grade: if any sentient being upholds the five precepts, observes the eight precepts of the fast, practices the various precepts, commits none of the five heinous offenses, and has no excess of faults and evil, then with these roots of goodness he dedicates them and vows to seek rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

The Buddha told Ānanda and Queen Vaidehī: As for those of the highest stage of the middle grade: if any sentient being upholds the five precepts, observes the eight precepts of the one-day fast, practices the various precepts, commits none of the five heinous offenses, and has no excess of faults and evil, then with these roots of goodness he dedicates them and vows to seek rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

The five precepts: not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct, not speaking falsely, and not drinking alcohol. First, not killing — not destroying the lives of sentient beings; second, not stealing — not taking the property of others; third, not committing sexual misconduct — not engaging in sexual acts apart from those between husband and wife; fourth, not speaking falsely — not uttering deceitful, misleading words; fifth, not drinking alcohol — not consuming intoxicating liquors or drugs. The five heinous offenses: these are five kinds of crimes supremely contrary to reason — killing one's father, killing one's mother, killing an arhat, causing blood to flow from the Buddha's body, and causing a schism in the Sangha. Because these five are acts of extreme evil, and the commission of any one of them leads to the avici hell, they are also called the 'avici karma.'

When the practicer is about to end his life, Amitābha Buddha, surrounded by the assembly of monks and his retinue, emitting golden light, comes to the place where this person is, and proclaims suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self, and praises leaving the household life and attaining release from all suffering.

[The practitioner, having seen this, is filled with great joy. He sees his own body seated upon a lotus throne; kneeling upright with palms joined, he makes obeisance to the Buddha. Before he has even lifted his head, he is instantly reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and the lotus opens at once. As the blossom unfolds, he hears a host of voices praising the Four Noble Truths, and in that very moment he attains the way of the arhat, together with the three insights and the six supernormal powers, and fully realizes the eight liberations. This is called the upper-grade rebirth of the middle rank.]

[The opening of the flower] refers to the unfolding of the lotus blossom. [The Four Noble Truths] are the four noble truths: the truth of suffering, the truth of its arising, the truth of its cessation, and the truth of the path. First, the “truth of suffering” sets forth the principle that life is replete with suffering. Suffering has the characteristic of oppression and affliction. In life there are three kinds of suffering, eight kinds of suffering, and immeasurable sufferings; suffering is the true condition of actual life. Second, the “arising” in “the truth of arising” means summoning and producing; it sets forth the principle of how the suffering of life comes about. The pain of life arises from craving, and so there is grasping; and so there is the creating of karma; and so there is suffering; and so there is the turning of the wheel of rebirth. Third, the “truth of cessation” sets forth the principle of bringing all suffering to an end. When all the arising of suffering (craving) is forever cut off without remainder, with no grasping and no clinging, one no longer creates karma, no longer suffers, no longer turns in the round — this is the truth of cessation. Fourth, the “truth of the path” sets forth how to forever cut off the arising of suffering (craving); this is the path that extinguishes suffering. Among the four noble truths, arising is the cause and suffering is the fruit; the path is the cause and cessation is the fruit.

[The four fruits of the sravaka] are the four fruits of the sravaka vehicle: the fruit of srotapanna, the fruit of sakrdagamin, the fruit of anagamin, and the fruit of the arhat. The first fruit, srotapanna, is rendered in Chinese as “enterer of the stream,” meaning one who first enters the stream of the sages. The second fruit, sakrdagamin, is rendered in Chinese as “one who returns once,” meaning that one who has reached this stage, after death, ascends to heaven and passes one life as a heavenly being, then is born once more in our world, and thereafter no longer comes to the desire realm to undergo birth and death. The third fruit, anagamin, is rendered in Chinese as “one who does not return,” meaning that one who has reached this stage will in the future be born in the form realm and the formless realm, and no longer come to the desire realm to undergo birth and death. The fourth fruit, the arhat, is rendered in Chinese as “one who is not born,” meaning that one who has reached this stage is released from birth and death and no longer receives a future existence, and is the highest fruit of the sravaka vehicle. [The sravaka] is one who, hearing the sound of the Buddha preaching the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, attains the Way.

[The three insights] are the insight into past lives, the divine eye, and the insight into the exhaustion of defilements. The insight into past lives is the clear knowledge of all the past lives of oneself and of others. The divine eye is the clear knowledge of all the future lives of oneself and of others. The insight into the exhaustion of defilements (asravakshaya) is the cutting off of all afflictions by means of the noble wisdom. [The six supernormal powers] are the divine eye, the divine ear, the knowledge of others’ minds, the knowledge of past lives, the power of spiritual manifestation, and the insight into the exhaustion of defilements. In detail: first, the divine eye, which can see the beings of the nine realms, the states of bliss and suffering in their passing from one life to another, and all the various forms and colors in the world, without any obstruction. Second, the divine ear, which can hear the words of joy and sorrow, pleasure and pain of the beings of the nine realms, and all the various sounds of the world. Third, the knowledge of others’ minds, which can know the thoughts that arise in the minds of the beings of the nine realms. Fourth, the knowledge of past lives, which can know one’s own past lives for one life, two lives, three lives, up to a hundred thousand and ten thousand lives, and the deeds done therein, and likewise can know the past lives and deeds of every sentient being. Fifth, the power of spiritual manifestation (the power of the wish-fulfilling body), whereby the body can fly over mountains and seas without obstruction, vanish from this world and emerge in another, vanish from that world and emerge in this; the great can be made small and the small great, transforming at will. Sixth, the insight into the exhaustion of defilements, which cuts off all afflictions (the delusions of views and of thought); “defilement” here means affliction. [The delusions of views and of thought] are the delusion of views and the delusion of thought. The delusion of views is the confusion of ordinary beings in their views, such as the five erroneous views: the view of a self, the view of extremes, the wrong view, the view of grasping to views, and the view of clinging to precepts and practices. The delusion of thought is the confusion of ordinary beings in their thoughts, such as the afflictions of greed, anger, delusion, pride, and doubt. These two delusions are the root cause of sentient beings’ wandering through the three realms and vainly undergoing birth and death; cutting them off, one can end birth and death and escape the three realms.

[The three realms] are the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm. The desire realm is the world in which beings still possessed of the two desires for sex and food dwell, including from the six heavens of desire above, through humans and animals, down to the hungry ghosts and hells. The form realm is the world in which beings free of the two desires of sex and food but still possessed of physical form dwell, including the four dhyana heavens numbering eighteen. The formless realm is the world in which beings who no longer have physical form dwell, abiding in mind-consciousness in deep meditative concentration, including the four heavens of emptiness (the heaven of infinite space, the heaven of infinite consciousness, the heaven of nothingness, and the heaven of neither-perception-nor-non-perception). These three realms are all the states in which ordinary beings undergo birth and death, and so the Buddhist practitioner first makes the renunciation of the three realms and the ending of birth and death his aim.

blocks.text: (2) The Middle-Grade Rebirth of the Middle Rank

inline.s: [In the middle-grade rebirth of the middle rank, if a sentient being observes the eight precepts of fasting for one day and one night, or observes the sramanera precepts for one day and one night, or observes the full precepts for one day and one night, with flawless deportment, and dedicates this merit with the vow to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, this observation perfumed and cultivated by the fragrance of the precepts.]

[The sramanera precepts] are the ten precepts observed by the sramanera: the precept against killing, the precept against stealing, the precept against sexual misconduct, the precept against false speech, the precept against drinking wine, the precept against sitting on a high and broad bed, the precept against wearing flowers and garlands, the precept against singing and dancing, the precept against gold and precious things, and the precept against eating at improper times. [The full precepts] are the complete and perfect precepts, such as the two hundred and fifty precepts of the bhikshu and the three hundred and forty-eight precepts of the bhikshuni.

[Such a practitioner, at the moment his life is about to end, sees Amitābha Buddha together with his assembly, emitting a golden light, holding a lotus of the seven jewels, and coming before him. The practitioner himself hears a voice in the sky praising him: “Good man, since you are a good person who accords with the teachings of the Buddhas of the three times, I have come to welcome you.”]

Such a practitioner, at the moment his life is about to end, sees Amitābha Buddha together with his assembly, emitting a golden light, holding a lotus of the seven jewels, and coming before him. The practitioner himself hears a voice in the sky praising him: “Good man, you are a good person who accords with the teaching of the Buddhas of the three times, and so I have come to welcome you.”

[The practitioner sees himself seated upon the lotus, and the lotus immediately closes, and he is born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. In the jewel pond, after seven days, the lotus opens. When the blossom has opened, he opens his eyes and joins his palms, praising the World-honored One. Hearing the Dharma he rejoices, and attains srotapanna; after half a kalpa he becomes an arhat. This is called the middle-grade rebirth of the middle rank.]

The practitioner sees himself seated upon the lotus, and the lotus immediately closes, and he is born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. In the pond of the seven jewels, after seven days, the lotus opens. When the blossom has opened, he opens his eyes, joins his palms, and praises the World-honored One. Hearing the Dharma he gives rise to joy and attains srotapanna; after half a kalpa he becomes an arhat. This is called the middle-grade rebirth of the middle rank.

blocks.text: (3) The Lower-Grade Rebirth of the Middle Rank

inline.s: [In the lower-grade rebirth of the middle rank, if a good man or a good woman supports and honors their parents and practices benevolence and righteousness in the world, and if this person, at the point his life is about to end, meets a good spiritual friend who speaks at length of the blissful matters of the land of Amitābha Buddha and also speaks of the forty-eight great vows of the Bhikshu Dharmakara — having heard these matters, this person immediately passes away, and as quickly as a strong man bends and stretches his arm, is born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.]

In the lower-grade rebirth of the middle rank, if a good man or a good woman supports and honors their parents and practices benevolence and righteousness in dealing with others, and if this person, at the point his life is about to end, meets a good spiritual friend who speaks at length of the blissful matters of the land of Amitābha Buddha and also tells of the forty-eight great vows of the Bhikshu Dharmakara — having heard these matters, this person immediately passes away, and as quickly as in the bending and stretching of a strong man’s arm, is born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

[The Bhikshu Dharmakara] is the name that Amitābha Buddha bore when, in his causal stage, he left home under the Buddha Free-and-Self-Mastery King of the World and practiced the bodhisattva path. [The forty-eight vows] are the forty-eight vows that Amitābha Buddha made before the Buddha Free-and-Self-Mastery King of the World when, on the causal ground, he was the Bhikshu Dharmakara; they are the blueprint for establishing the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. [As a strong man bends and stretches his arm] describes the shortness of the time.

[After seven days have passed, he meets Avalokitesvara and Mahasthamaprapta, and hearing the Dharma he rejoices and attains srotapanna; after one small kalpa he becomes an arhat. This is called the lower-grade rebirth of the middle rank.]

After seven days have passed, he meets Bodhisattva Avalokitesvara and Bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta, who preach the Dharma to him; hearing the Dharma he rejoices and is illumined, and attains the fruit of srotapanna; after one small kalpa he attains the fruit of the arhat. This is called the lower-grade rebirth of the middle rank.
[This is called the contemplation of the middle-grade rebirth, and is known as the fifteenth contemplation.]

The contemplation of the three states of rebirth above (the upper-grade, the middle-grade, and the lower-grade rebirths of the middle rank) is together called the contemplation of the middle-grade rebirth, and is the fifteenth contemplation.

blocks.text: 16. The Contemplation of the Lower-Grade Rebirth (Contemplating the Multitude of Beings)
(1) The Upper-Grade Rebirth of the Lower Rank

inline.s: [The Buddha told Ānanda and Vaidehī: In the upper-grade rebirth of the lower rank, there may be beings who commit many evil deeds. Though they do not slander the scriptures of the Great Vehicle, such foolish beings perpetrate many evil dharmas and have no sense of shame.]

The Buddha told Ānanda and Vaidehī: In the upper-grade rebirth of the lower rank, there may be beings who commit many evil deeds. Although they do not slander the Mahayana scriptures, such foolish beings perpetrate many evil dharmas and have no sense of shame.
[An evil dharma] is a wrong view that slanders wholesome dharmas.

[At the point his life is about to end, he meets a good spiritual friend who praises the titles of the twelve divisions of the Great Vehicle scriptures. Because he hears the names of these scriptures, he wipes away the extremely heavy evil karma of a thousand kalpas. The wise one further teaches him to join his palms and, with his fingers interlaced, to say ‘Namo Amitābha Buddha’; and because he calls upon the Buddha’s name, he wipes away the karma of birth and death of five billions of kalpas.]

At the point his life is about to end, he meets a wise good spiritual friend who praises the titles of the twelve divisions of the Great Vehicle scriptures; and because he hears the names of these scriptures, he wipes away the extremely heavy evil karma of a thousand kalpas. The good spiritual friend further teaches him to join his palms and, with his fingers interlaced, to call upon ‘Namo Amitābha Buddha’; and because he calls upon the Buddha’s name, he wipes away the karma of birth and death of five billions of kalpas.

[At that time that Buddha thereupon sends an emanated Buddha, an emanated Avalokitesvara, and an emanated Mahasthamaprapta, to come before the practitioner and say: “How wonderful! Good man, because you have called upon the Buddha’s name, all your offenses are eradicated, and I have come to welcome you.”]

At that time Amitābha Buddha thereupon sends an emanated Buddha, an emanated Bodhisattva Avalokitesvara, and an emanated Bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta, to come before the practitioner and say: “How wonderful! Good man, because you have called upon the Buddha’s name, all your offenses are eradicated, and I have come to welcome you.”
[All offenses eradicated] This shows that an evil person’s rebirth comes about only after all their offenses have been eradicated.

[Having spoken these words, the practitioner then sees the light of the emanated Buddha filling the whole room. Seeing it he rejoices, and at once passes away, and riding a jeweled lotus, following behind the emanated Buddha, is born in the jewel pond. After forty-nine days (seven times seven), the lotus opens.]

Having spoken these words, the practitioner then sees the light of the emanated Buddha filling the whole room. Seeing the light he is filled with joy, and at once passes away, and riding a jeweled lotus, following behind the emanated Buddha, is born in the pond of the seven jewels. After forty-nine days (seven times seven), the lotus opens.

[When the blossom opens, the Great Compassionate Bodhisattva Avalokitesvara and Bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta emit a great light, stand before the person, and preach the profound twelve divisions of the scriptures; hearing them, he believes and understands, and gives rise to the mind of the unexcelled Way. After ten small kalpas he becomes fully endowed with the hundred Dharma-gates of light and enters the first ground. This is called the upper-grade rebirth of the lower rank.]

When the blossom opens, the Great Compassionate Bodhisattva Avalokitesvara and Bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta emit a great light and stand before the person, preaching the profound twelve divisions of the scriptures; hearing them, he at once gives rise to faith and understanding and arouses the mind of the unexcelled Way. After ten small kalpas he realizes the hundred Dharma-gates of light and enters the first ground. This is called the upper-grade rebirth of the lower rank.

blocks.text: (2) The Middle-Grade Rebirth of the Lower Rank

inline.s: [The Buddha told Ānanda and Vaidehī: In the middle-grade rebirth of the lower rank, there may be beings who violate and break the five precepts, the eight precepts, and the full precepts. Such foolish beings steal the goods of the monastic community, steal the goods of the monks present, preach the Dharma impurely, have no sense of shame, and adorn themselves with all manner of evil dharmas. Such offenders, because of their evil karma, should fall into the hells.]

The Buddha told Ānanda and Vaidehī: In the middle-grade rebirth of the lower rank, there may be beings who violate and break the five precepts, the eight precepts, and the full precepts. Such foolish beings steal the goods of the community, steal the goods of the monks present, preach the Dharma impurely, have no sense of shame, and adorn themselves with all manner of evil dharmas. Such offenders, because of their evil karma, should fall into the hells.

[The goods of the monastic community] are the things belonging to the assembly as a whole. [Preaching the Dharma impurely] means distorting the right Dharma, or preaching with an impure mind. For instance, with some ulterior motive, speaking false words so as to induce belief, or not preaching the Buddha-Dharma at all but merely talking of worldly affairs. [Adorning] means to ornament a land with what is good and beautiful, or to adorn one’s body with merit and virtue. Again, heaping evil deeds upon one’s person is also called ‘adorning’; here ‘adorning’ has the sense of decorating and embellishing.

[At the point his life is about to end, the fires of the hells come upon them all at once. He meets a good spiritual friend who, with great compassion, praises the power and virtue of the ten powers of Amitābha Buddha, praises at length the light and spiritual power of that Buddha, and also praises precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge-and-vision of liberation. Having heard these, this person wipes away the karma of birth and death of eighty billions of kalpas, and the fierce fires of the hells are transformed into a cooling breeze that carries celestial flowers, upon each of which are emanated Buddhas and bodhisattvas welcoming this person.]

At the point his life is about to end, the fires of the hells come upon them all at once. He meets a wise good spiritual friend who, with great compassion, praises the power and virtue of the ten powers of Amitābha Buddha, praises at length the light and spiritual power of Amitābha Buddha, and also praises precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge-and-vision of liberation. Having heard these, this person wipes away the karma of birth and death of eighty billions of kalpas, and the fierce fires of the hells are transformed into a cooling breeze carrying celestial flowers, upon each of which are emanated Buddhas and bodhisattvas welcoming this person.

[In a single instant he is reborn within a lotus in the pond of the seven jewels. After six kalpas the lotus opens. When the blossom opens, Avalokitesvara and Mahasthamaprapta, with voices of Brahma sound, comfort that person and preach the profound scriptures of the Great Vehicle. Having heard this Dharma, he at once gives rise to the mind of the unexcelled Way. This is called the middle-grade rebirth of the lower rank.]

In a single instant he is reborn within a lotus in the pond of the seven jewels. After six kalpas the lotus opens. When the blossom opens, Bodhisattva Avalokitesvara and Bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta, with voices of Brahma sound, comfort him and preach the profound scriptures of the Great Vehicle. Having heard this Dharma, he at once gives rise to the mind of the unexcelled Way. This is called the middle-grade rebirth of the lower rank.

blocks.text: (2) The Lower-Grade Rebirth of the Lower Rank

inline.s: [The Buddha told Ānanda and Vaidehī: In the lower-grade rebirth of the lower rank, there may be beings who commit unwholesome deeds, the five rebellious acts and the ten evil deeds, and are replete with every unwholesome thing. Such foolish beings, because of their evil karma, should fall into the evil destinies, passing through many kalpas and undergoing immeasurable suffering.]

The Buddha told Ānanda and Lady Vaidehī: In the lower-grade rebirth of the lower rank, if there are beings who create evil deeds, the five rebellious acts and the ten evil deeds, stopping at nothing. Such foolish beings, because of their evil karma, should fall into the evil destinies, passing through many kalpas and undergoing immeasurable suffering.
[The ten evil deeds] are also called the ten unwholesome deeds, namely: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, idle talk, harsh speech, divisive speech, greed, anger, and delusion.

[Such a foolish person, at the end of his life, meets a good spiritual friend who comforts him in many ways, preaches the wondrous Dharma for him, and teaches him to be mindful of the Buddha. That person, pressed by suffering, has no leisure to be mindful of the Buddha; and the good companion tells him: “If you cannot be mindful of that Buddha, you should call upon the name of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life to whom you take refuge.” Thus with utmost sincerity he makes the sound of the name never cease, and with ten complete thoughts, says ‘Namo Amitābha Buddha’.]

Such a foolish person, at the end of his life, meets a wise good spiritual friend who comforts him in many ways, tells him of the excellence of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and of the great benefit of being reborn there, and teaches him to contemplate Amitābha Buddha so as to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. But because this person, with the signs of the hells appearing, has no leisure to settle his mind and contemplate the Buddha, the good companion says to him: “If you are unable to contemplate that Buddha, you should call upon the name of that Buddha. With utmost sincerity, single and unbroken, call upon ‘Namo Amitābha Buddha’, thought after thought continuing, and complete the ten sounds.”

[Teaching him to be mindful of the Buddha] means teaching him to contemplate Amitābha Buddha. Here ‘mindful’ means to fix the mind in contemplation. [Pressed by suffering] means the signs of the hells appear. [Leisure] means free time. [If you cannot be mindful of that Buddha, you should call upon the name of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life] Since this sutra (the Sutra of the Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life) is mainly about the recitation that contemplates the Buddha, the phrase ‘mindful of the Buddha’ refers to contemplation-recitation, whereas the calling upon the name is called ‘calling upon the Buddha.’ [Thus with utmost sincerity, making the sound of the name never cease] Unmixed and single is called ‘utmost sincerity’; continuing without a break is called ‘never cease.’ [Ten thoughts] means ten utterances of the Buddha’s name.
[Because he calls upon the Buddha’s name, in each thought he wipes away the karma of birth and death of eighty billions of kalpas.]
Because he thus continues the ten thoughts and calls upon the Buddha’s name, in every thought he extinguishes the karma of birth and death of eighty billions of kalpas.
As for the case of the lower-grade lower-rank person who attains rebirth through Buddha-recitation at death, Master Yinguang has instructed:
“In the Contemplation Sutra, one guilty of the five rebellious acts and the ten evil deeds, at the point his life is about to end, with the signs of the hells appearing, has a good spiritual friend
(The original note: this is regardless of monk or layman, man or woman; whoever can teach that person to be mindful of the Buddha is called a good spiritual friend.)

to teach him to be mindful of the Buddha — perhaps a full ten sounds, perhaps not even ten — and straightway he passes away, and yet, relying on the Buddha’s compassionate power, he is reborn while still bearing his karma. These ten thoughts, compared with the ordinary ten thoughts, have a force as different as heaven and the deep abyss; and so he gains rebirth. Because, pressed by the extreme suffering of the hells, the very moment he hears the Buddha’s name he calls upon it with his whole being and spirit.

Apart from this thought, there is absolutely no other thought. Though he has not personally realized the single-minded and undisturbed state, still his mind is in the end wholly free of any differing thought.
(The Collected Writings of Master Yinguang
Reply to the Layman Chen Xinru)
Master Shandao, in his Commentary on the Four Sections of the Contemplation Sutra, explains the meaning of the ‘Chapter on the Lower-Grade Lower Rebirth’ as follows:

“From ‘such a foolish person’ down to ‘the karma of birth and death’, it precisely sets forth the present benefit gained by hearing the Dharma and being mindful of the Buddha, and there are ten points: first, it sets forth the renewed mention of the person who has committed evil; second, it sets forth that his life is short and not long; third, it sets forth that at death he meets a good spiritual friend; fourth, it sets forth that the good person comforts him and teaches him to be mindful of the Buddha; fifth, it sets forth that the offender, pressed by the suffering of death, has no way to be mindful of the Buddha’s name; sixth, it sets forth that the good companion, knowing his suffering and the loss of his mindfulness, turns to teach him to call aloud the name of Amitābha; seventh, it sets forth the number of recollections,
sound after sound without any break
; eighth, it sets forth the wiping away of offenses of many kalpas; ninth,
it sets forth that right mindfulness at death brings the golden lotus to respond
(This points out: right mindfulness at death, and the golden lotus comes to respond)
; tenth, it sets forth the slowness or swiftness of the departing, straight to the land to which he returns.”
Please pay special attention to what Master Shandao says here:
rebirth through right mindfulness at death
(‘it sets forth that right mindfulness at death brings the golden lotus to respond’).
Please pay particular attention to Master Shandao, who in his instruction says: “
sound after sound without any break
” and “
right mindfulness at death, and the golden lotus comes to welcome

”. Since it is ‘right mindfulness at death’, this shows that at the time of death-recitation there is no admixture of deluded thoughts. Since there is no admixture of deluded thoughts, therefore the ‘
sound after sound without any break

’ is the very thought of Buddha-recitation, thought after thought continuing without a break. Therefore, this person guilty of the five rebellious acts and the ten evil deeds, at death, has the thought of Buddha-recitation continuing thought after thought — right mindfulness at death — and so extinguishes his offenses and gains rebirth. Regarding this, Master Daochuo in his Collection of Peace and Bliss also instructs:
At the time when all sentient beings approach death
, the wind of the sword dissolves the body, the suffering of death presses upon them, and great terror arises. Therefore, meeting a good spiritual friend, they rouse great courage and vigor,
and with thought after thought continuing through ten recollections
, which is the superior root of goodness,
and they then gain rebirth
Moreover, taking up the ‘
sound after sound without any break
’ and the ‘
right mindfulness at death, and the golden lotus comes to welcome
’ together with Master Shandao’s instructions on ‘continuity brings rebirth’ and ‘right mindfulness at death’ (see in detail
Master Shandao’s Pure Land Teaching
, that article) and reading them together, one clearly understands that when Master Shandao, in his Commentary on the Four Sections of the Contemplation Sutra, says
“But if one can, from the whole of one’s life down to a single thought of ten recollections, by the Buddha’s vow-power, all are reborn — hence it is called the easy path”
and in his Praise of Rebirth says
If I attain Buddhahood, and beings in the ten directions, calling upon my name, down to a single ten sounds, if they are not reborn, then I will not attain perfect enlightenment”
, the phrase ‘down to ten thoughts’ in these passages
refers to the ten thoughts continuing without break at death

[At the time of death, he sees a golden lotus, like the wheel of the sun, resting before him; in a single instant he is reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Within the lotus he remains for a full twelve great kalpas, and only then does the lotus open. When the blossom opens, Avalokitesvara and Mahasthamaprapta, with the sound of great compassion, at once broadly expound for him the reality of all dharmas and the Dharma that extinguishes offenses; hearing this he rejoices, and at once gives rise to the bodhi mind. This is called the lower-grade rebirth of the lower rank.]

At the time of death, he sees a golden lotus, like the wheel of the sun, resting before him. In a single instant he is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Within the lotus he remains for a full twelve great kalpas, and only then does the lotus open. At that time, Bodhisattva Avalokitesvara and Bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta, with the sound of great compassion, broadly expound for him the reality of all dharmas and the Dharma that extinguishes offenses. Having heard this, he joyfully receives it with faith, and at once gives rise to the bodhi mind. This is called the lower-grade rebirth of the lower rank.

[The Dharma that extinguishes offenses through the reality of all dharmas] is the Dharma by which, through the reality of all dharmas, all offenses are extinguished. The Sutra of the Contemplation of the Bodhisattva Universal Virtue says:

“The ocean of all karmic hindrances is born entirely from deluded thought. If one wishes to repent, sit upright and be mindful of reality. All offenses are as frost and dew; the sun of wisdom can dispel them.”

[Giving rise to the bodhi mind] means to arouse the bodhi mind. ‘Bodhi’ is rendered in Chinese as ‘awakening.’ [Giving rise to the bodhi mind] To arouse the bodhi mind, whose full name is ‘to arouse the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.’ The bodhi mind is the mind of pure self-nature. This mind of pure self-nature is equal in sentient beings and Buddhas, possessed by all, neither increasing nor decreasing. ‘Arouse’ means to initiate, to bring forth. To arouse the bodhi mind is to initiate and bring forth the mind of pure self-nature. The first arousal is merely the initiating; seeing one’s nature is what is called the bringing forth. [Seeing one’s nature] means to see through to the original nature.
[This is called the contemplation of the lower-grade rebirth, and is the sixteenth contemplation.]

The contemplation of the three states of rebirth above (the upper-grade, the middle-grade, and the lower-grade rebirths of the lower rank) is together called the contemplation of the lower-grade rebirth, and is the fourteenth contemplation.

blocks.text: 3. Receiving, Upholding, and Spreading the Teaching

inline.s: This chapter is the transmission section of this sutra, setting forth the receiving, upholding, and spreading abroad of this sutra.

blocks.text: 1. All Shall Be Reborn

inline.s: [At that time, when the World-honored One spoke these words, Vaidehī and her five hundred maid-servants, hearing what the Buddha said, at once saw the vast and square aspect of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and beheld the body of the Buddha and the two bodhisattvas. Their minds gave rise to joy, and they declared that they had never before seen such a thing; they were suddenly and greatly awakened, and attained the patience of non-production.]

At that time, when the World-honored One finished preaching this sutra, Vaidehī and her five hundred maid-servants, hearing what the Buddha said, at once saw the vast and square aspect of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and beheld the golden body of Amitābha Buddha and the two bodhisattvas, Avalokitesvara and Mahasthamaprapta. Their minds gave rise to joy, and they declared that they had never before seen such a thing; they were suddenly and greatly awakened, destroying their ignorance, and attained the patience of non-production.
[Attaining the patience of non-production] means to gain the patience of non-production. ‘Attain’ means to obtain. The preceding scripture says:

“By the Buddha’s power, they shall see that pure land, as one holding a bright mirror sees one’s own face. Seeing the supremely wondrous and blissful things of that land, their minds rejoice, and at once they attain the patience of the non-production of dharmas.”

[The five hundred maid-servants gave rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, and vowed to be born in that land. The World-honored One gave the prophecy to them all, that they should all be reborn there; and having been born in that land, they attained the samādhi of the Buddhas appearing before them. The countless devas gave rise to the mind of the unexcelled Way.]

The five hundred maid-servants gave rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, and vowed to be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. The World-honored One gave them the prophecy that they should all be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Having been born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, they at once attained the samādhi of the Buddhas appearing before them. The countless devas and humans likewise gave rise to the mind of the unexcelled Way.
[Giving rise to the mind of the unexcelled Way] means giving rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.

blocks.text: 2. How to Receive and Uphold the Teaching

inline.s: [At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat, came before the Buddha, and said: World-honored One, what should this sutra be named? What is the essential of this Dharma, and how should it be received and upheld?]

At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat, came before the Buddha, and said: ‘World-honored One, what is the name of this sutra? What is the essential of this Dharma, and how should one receive and uphold it?’
[The essential of this Dharma, how should it be received and upheld] In the following, the World-honored One answers:
“You must hold well to these words! Whoever holds to these words is thereby upholding the Name of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life.”

Therefore, the answer to ‘the essential of this Dharma (the essential of this sutra’s teaching)’ is: holding and reciting the Buddha’s name. The answer to ‘how should it be received and upheld (how should one receive and uphold it)’ is: holding and reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha.
Regarding ‘whoever holds to these words is thereby upholding the Name of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life’, Master Shandao instructs:

“Question: Why did he not have them contemplate, but directly sends them to single-mindedly call upon the Name? Answer: Beings have heavy hindrances; the object (the realm contemplated) is subtle while the mind is coarse, the consciousness wanders and the spirit flies about, so that contemplation is hard to accomplish. Therefore the Great Sage
(Śākyamuni Buddha)

, with compassionate pity, directly urges them to single-mindedly call upon the Name. Precisely because calling upon the Name is easy, continuity brings rebirth. If one can practice thought after thought continuing, taking the end of one’s life as the limit
(the person who thus practices to the end of life)

, then of ten, ten are reborn; of a hundred, a hundred are reborn. Why? Because there are no outer sundry conditions and one gains right mindfulness; because it accords with the Buddha’s primal vow; because it does not violate the teaching; because it complies with the Buddha’s words.”
(The Special and Sundry Practice of Pure Karma)
Translation:

Question: Why did Śākyamuni Buddha, in the Sutra of the Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, not have them contemplate (this refers to the thirteen contemplations in the sutra, such as the contemplation of the sun and the contemplation of the water), but directly teaches them to single-mindedly call upon the Name? Answer: Beings’ karmic hindrances are deep and heavy; the object (the realm contemplated) is subtle while the mind is coarse, the consciousness wanders and the spirit flies about, so that meditation on the contemplation is hard to accomplish. Therefore Śākyamuni Buddha, with compassionate pity, directly teaches them to single-mindedly call upon the name of Amitābha Buddha. Precisely because holding the name and being mindful of the Buddha is easier to accomplish than contemplating the Buddha, at the moment of death one need only make the thought of Buddha-recitation continue without a break (not interrupted by deluded thoughts), and one is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. If one can make the thought of Buddha-recitation continue, and thus practice to the end of one’s life, then of ten people ten are reborn, and of a hundred, a hundred are reborn. Why? Because, single-mindedly calling upon the Name, the mind does not turn outward to sundry conditions (the mind does not vainly grasp at all manner of sundry outer things), and so one gains right mindfulness; because it accords with the primal vow of Amitābha Buddha; because it does not violate the teaching of Śākyamuni Buddha; because it complies with the holy words of Śākyamuni Buddha.

[Continuity brings rebirth] ‘Continuity brings rebirth’ means this: at the time of death, if the thought of Buddha-recitation continues without a break (not interrupted by deluded thoughts), one is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. The ‘continuity’ here is the ‘pure thought continuing on without a break’ spoken of in the Chapter on the Perfect and Universal Penetration of the Buddha-remembrance of the Bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta, that is, the thought of Buddha-recitation, thought after thought continuing, with no deluded thought mixed in between (if deluded thought is mixed in, it is not continuity). One must by no means misread the two words ‘continuity’ here as the mere continuity of the Buddha’s name on the lips (while the mind is given over to deluded thought). This is what is called: a divergence of a hair’s breadth leads to an error of a thousand miles. [Thought after thought continuing, taking the end of one’s life as the limit] Because at the time of death the continuation of the thought of Buddha-recitation brings rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, one must thus practice to the end of one’s life, making the thought of Buddha-recitation continue until it becomes a settled nature through repeated practice. In this way one is certain to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss — of ten, ten are reborn; of a hundred, a hundred are reborn. [Becoming a settled nature through repeated practice] means, through constant and repeated practice, making the thought of Buddha-recitation and its continuation become an instinctive nature.

[The Buddha told Ānanda: This sutra is named the Contemplation of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, the Bodhisattva Avalokitesvara, and the Bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta; it is also named the Washing Away of Karmic Hindrances and Being Born Before the Buddhas.]

The Buddha told Ānanda: This sutra is named the Contemplation of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, the Bodhisattva Avalokitesvara, and the Bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta; it is also named the Washing Away of Karmic Hindrances and Being Born Before the Buddhas.

blocks.text: 3. The Washing Away of the Karma of Birth and Death

inline.s: [You should receive and uphold it, and do not let it be lost. Whoever practices this samādhi, in this very life, sees the Buddha of Immeasurable Life and the two great beings. If a good man or a good woman, merely by hearing the name of the Buddha and the names of the two bodhisattvas, wipes away the karma of birth and death of immeasurable kalpas — how much the more so if they are mindful of it!]

You should receive and uphold this sutra, and do not let it be lost. Whoever practices this samādhi, in this very life, sees the Buddha of Immeasurable Life and the two great beings, the Bodhisattva Avalokitesvara and the Bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta. If a good man or a good woman, merely by hearing the name of the Buddha and the names of the two bodhisattvas, wipes away the karma of birth and death of immeasurable kalpas — how much the more so if they are mindful of the Buddha’s name!

[If one is mindful of the Buddha, know that such a person is the pundarika lotus flower among humans; the Bodhisattva Avalokitesvara and the Bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta are his excellent companions, and he shall sit at the place of enlightenment and be born in the family of the Buddhas.]

If there is one who is mindful of the Buddha, know that such a person is the pundarika lotus flower among humans; the Bodhisattva Avalokitesvara and the Bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta are his excellent companions, and he shall sit at the place of enlightenment and be born in the family of the Buddhas (meaning that he will certainly accomplish Buddhahood).

[The pundarika flower] is rendered in meaning as the white lotus. This flower grows in the mud yet is not defiled by the mud, and so the scriptures and treatises often use it as a simile for the Buddha-nature, which dwells amid afflictions yet is not defiled by them. [The place of enlightenment] is the place where enlightenment is accomplished. [Being born in the family of the Buddhas] means to be born in the family of the Buddhas. The word ‘zhu’ here has the sense of ‘into’ or ‘unto.’ For example: ‘When he cast it into the far reaches of the Bohai Sea.’ (Liezi
Tang’s Question)

blocks.text: 4. Holding the Buddha’s Name

inline.s: [The Buddha told Ānanda: You must hold well to these words! Whoever holds to these words is thereby upholding the Name of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life.]
The Buddha told Ānanda: You must receive and uphold well this sutra that I have taught! To receive and uphold this sutra is to hold and recite the name of Amitābha Buddha.
This passage is the Buddha’s answer to Ānanda’s question above: ‘What is the essential of this Dharma, and how should it be received and upheld?’
Master Shandao says in his Commentary on the Four Sections of the Contemplation Sutra:

“From ‘The Buddha told Ānanda: You must hold well to these words’ onward, this precisely sets forth the entrusting of the Name of Amitābha, to be spread abroad through distant generations. Although I have explained above the benefits of the two gates of meditative and non-meditative good, looking to the Buddha’s fundamental vow, the intent is that sentient beings should single-mindedly and exclusively recite the name of Amitābha Buddha.”

(Translation: The passage of scripture that reads, “The Buddha told Ānanda: You must hold well to these words! Whoever holds to these words is thereby upholding the Name of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life,” precisely indicates that this sutra is the World-honored One’s entrustment to Ānanda: that he should spread abroad the practice of holding the name and being mindful of the Buddha (calling upon the name of Amitābha Buddha) down to distant generations. Although the scripture above taught the benefits of the two gates of meditative and non-meditative good, in the light of Śākyamuni Buddha’s fundamental vow, the intent lies in sentient beings’ single-mindedly and exclusively calling upon the name of Amitābha Buddha.)

[The two gates of meditative and non-meditative good] In his Commentary on the Four Sections of the Contemplation Sutra, Master Shandao divides the sixteen contemplations into these two gates, meditative good and non-meditative good: the first thirteen contemplations (from the contemplation of the sun to the contemplation of miscellaneous forms) contemplate, with a mind of meditative concentration, the dependent and primary rewards of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and are therefore called “meditative good”; the last three contemplations cultivate the practices of the three blessings and the nine grades with a mind that is not concentrated in meditation, and are therefore called “non-meditative good.” [Single-mindedly and exclusively calling upon the name of Amitābha Buddha] This is the “single-minded exclusive recitation” spoken of in the Sutra of Immeasurable Life: always holding the name and being mindful of the Buddha with one mind, with no divergent thoughts. (For details, see the article
Single-Minded Exclusive Recitation
[When the Buddha spoke these words, the venerable Maudgalyayana, the venerable Ānanda, and Vaidehī and the others, hearing what the Buddha said, were all filled with great joy.]

When the World-honored One had finished preaching this sutra, the venerable Maudgalyayana, the venerable Ānanda, and Vaidehī and the others, hearing what the Buddha said, were all filled with great joy.
The above is the World-honored One preaching the Dharma to Vaidehī and the others in the palace of her confinement.

blocks.text: 5. Ānanda Speaks It Forth

inline.s: What follows is the venerable Ānanda, on Mount Grdhrakuta (Vulture Peak), proclaiming this sutra to the holy assembly on the Buddha’s behalf.
[At that time, the World-honored One walked upon the air and returned to Mount Grdhrakuta.]
At that time, the World-honored One trod upon the air and returned to Mount Grdhrakuta.

[At that time, Ānanda widely proclaimed to the great assembly the matters set forth above. Measureless devas, nagas, and yaksas, hearing what the Buddha had said, were all filled with great joy, bowed to the Buddha, and withdrew.]

At that time, the venerable Ānanda widely proclaimed the matters set forth above to the great assembly (the great assembly of monks, twelve hundred and fifty in all, together with the thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas, with Bodhisattva Manjusri as their leader). Measureless devas, nagas, and yaksas, having heard this sutra spoken by the Buddha, were all filled with great joy, bowed to the Buddha, and withdrew.
